stories.headline: COP31 ends without a deal as fossil fuel divisions deepen
stories.summary: COP31, held in Antalya, Türkiye, ended without a major deal after talks ran into record extra time, breaking down two days past their scheduled close. The central deadlock was over whether the outcome text should mention fossil fuels; the EU refused to endorse an 'Antalya Pact' that did not mention them, while other parties resisted such language. Divisions over climate finance also deepened, and the COP31 President drew criticism from civil society for calling it the 'best COP ever' amid the deadlock. No substantive agreement was reached, raising fresh questions about the future of consensus-based UN climate negotiations.
stories.whyItMatters: The outcome tests the viability of the UNFCCC process, the principle of CBDR-RC, and the politics of fossil fuel phase-out and climate finance — core themes for GS-III environment and GS-II global governance. It also provides a live case study for prelims on COP outcomes and multilateral deadlocks.

static.topic: Climate Change Regime & India's Commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change
static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle. The Paris Agreement uses NDCs and a ratchet mechanism. The Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and LiFE mission.
static.geography: Global (UNFCCC process); India-specific targets and commitments.
static.socioEconomic: Climate finance and technology transfer gaps affect developing countries' mitigation and adaptation capacity; equity and just transition concerns remain central.
static.whyInNews: COP31 in Antalya ended without a major deal, with divisions over fossil fuel language and climate finance deepening.
static.wayForward: Bridge climate finance and technology transfer gaps; ensure equity in the Global Stocktake and a just transition for developing economies.
prelimsPointers: India's updated NDC: cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 by 2030.
Paris Agreement goal: keep warming well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C.
static.mainsAngle: Climate finance and technology transfer gaps; examine equity in the Global Stocktake and just transition.

static.topic: United Nations & Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: The collapse of COP31 talks without a deal highlights the limits of consensus-based multilateralism and the difficulty of reconciling divergent interests.
static.wayForward: Strengthen multilateral institutions and consensus mechanisms; advance reform, including UNSC expansion, to enhance representativeness and effectiveness.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN HQ is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim rests on representativeness, its population and contributions; assess obstacles (veto politics, Africa's Ezulwini Consensus).

stories.headline: India and EU set to sign free trade pact on December 16 in Brussels
stories.summary: India and the European Union are set to sign their long-pending free trade agreement on December 16, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi's scheduled Brussels visit expected to seal the deal. The announcement was indicated by the EU's Ambassador to India, Jean-Eric Paquet, who said the agreement would come into force in 2027. The pact caps nearly two decades of stop-start negotiations that began in 2007, were suspended in 2013 and relaunched in 2022. The timing places the agreement within a wider churn in India's external economic policy, as New Delhi simultaneously manages a rivalrous China relationship and a European bloc increasingly assertive on carbon and sustainability standards.
stories.whyItMatters: A concluded India-EU FTA would be one of India's largest trade deals, reshaping tariff, services and investment access with its biggest goods trading partner and giving New Delhi a template for balancing strategic autonomy against European regulatory demands.

perspectives.take: Frames the Brussels visit primarily as a diplomatic achievement for PM Modi, presenting the December 16 signing as the culmination of sustained high-level political push.
Reports the development procedurally, anchoring it to the EU Ambassador's statement and flagging the 2027 entry into force, i.e. ratification and implementation remain ahead.

Think-tank framing that situates the FTA within the wider India–China–EU triangle, reading the deal as part of a fragmented-world strategy of partnerships and rivalries rather than a standalone trade event.

static.topic: India–EU Free Trade Agreement (BTIA)
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral and Regional Trade Agreements
static.whatIsIt: A proposed comprehensive bilateral trade and investment agreement between India and the European Union, negotiated as the Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement (BTIA). It is envisaged to cover trade in goods, services, investment, intellectual property, government procurement and sustainable development provisions.
static.background: Negotiations were launched in 2007 but stalled in 2013 over differences on tariffs, intellectual property, data security and market access. Talks were formally relaunched in June 2022 and have since proceeded through multiple negotiating rounds. The agreement is now slated for signature on December 16 during the Prime Minister's Brussels visit, with entry into force expected in 2027 after ratification.
static.geography: The European Union is a 27-member bloc and, as a single market, is India's largest trading partner in goods; the agreement would govern access across all member states.
static.socioEconomic: Indian defensive interests include textiles, leather, marine products, auto components and generic pharmaceuticals, while the EU seeks greater access for wines and spirits, automobiles and dairy. European sustainability measures such as the carbon border adjustment mechanism and the deforestation regulation are key Indian concerns.
static.whyInNews: The EU Ambassador to India, Jean-Eric Paquet, stated that the FTA will be signed during PM Modi's December visit to Brussels and will come into force in 2027.
static.wayForward: Resolution of outstanding issues on carbon and sustainability-linked trade measures, geographical indications, data adequacy and Mode 4 mobility; a separate investment protection framework; and ratification by the European Parliament and member states.
prelimsPointers: The EU is India's largest trading partner in goods; FTA talks began in 2007, were suspended in 2013 and relaunched in 2022.
The agreement is expected to be signed on December 16 and to enter into force in 2027.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate how the India–EU FTA advances India's trade diversification and strategic autonomy while weighing the costs of accepting European labour, environment and carbon-linked conditionalities.

static.topic: India–EU Strategic Partnership and Trade and Technology Council
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and Major Powers and Groupings
static.whatIsIt: The India–EU Strategic Partnership, established in 2004, is the umbrella political framework for summit-level dialogue, sectoral cooperation and the Roadmap to 2025. The Trade and Technology Council (TTC) is a ministerial-level mechanism with working groups on technology, digital and trade issues.
static.background: The strategic partnership dates to 2004 and has been progressively institutionalised through annual summits and a Roadmap to 2025. The TTC was announced in 2022 and first met at the ministerial level in Brussels in May 2023, adding a structured track for technology, digital governance and resilient supply chains.
static.geography: The EU is a supranational union of 27 member states whose executive arm is the European Commission; the EU delegation in New Delhi is the bloc's diplomatic mission in India.
static.socioEconomic: The partnership extends beyond trade to clean energy, digital public infrastructure, research and connectivity, with the EU positioning itself as a partner in de-risking supply chains away from concentrated dependence.
static.whyInNews: The December 16 signing of the FTA is the headline outcome of the broader strategic partnership and follows sustained engagement through summitry and the TTC.
static.wayForward: Sustaining momentum through the TTC on technology and digital standards, aligning connectivity initiatives in the Indo-Pacific, and managing divergence on Russia and China without eroding the trade track.
prelimsPointers: India and the EU elevated ties to a Strategic Partnership in 2004; the Trade and Technology Council first met at ministerial level in Brussels in May 2023.
The European Commission is the EU's executive; the EU has 27 member states.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how institutional mechanisms such as the TTC complement a trade agreement in building a durable India–EU partnership amid great-power competition.

static.topic: EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and Green Trade Measures
static.syllabusNode: Economy — External Sector and Environment — Climate and Trade Linkages
static.whatIsIt: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is an EU levy on the embedded carbon content of carbon-intensive imports, designed to prevent carbon leakage. It applies to cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen.
static.background: CBAM is part of the EU Green Deal and the Fit for 55 package, building on the EU Emissions Trading System. A transitional reporting phase ran from October 2023 to the end of 2025, with the definitive levy regime applying from January 2026. India has raised concerns in multilateral forums about its consistency with equity and common but differentiated responsibilities.
static.geography: Applies uniformly to imports into the EU single market, affecting exporters in India, and is administered by the European Commission.
static.socioEconomic: Indian steel, aluminium and cement exporters face added compliance and cost burdens; the measure is viewed in India as a trade barrier dressed as climate policy, with implications for MSMEs in downstream sectors.
static.whyInNews: CBAM and the EU deforestation regulation are among the most contested issues in the India–EU trade negotiations now heading to signature.
static.wayForward: Seek recognition of equivalent Indian carbon pricing and monitoring systems, negotiate transitional relief for MSME exporters, and pursue the issue through WTO and UNFCCC processes while domestic decarbonisation proceeds.
prelimsPointers: CBAM covers cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen; the definitive levy regime applies from January 2026.
The EU Emissions Trading System is the world's first major carbon market and underpins CBAM.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether unilateral carbon border measures are compatible with the UNFCCC's equity principles and assess India's options for protecting export competitiveness.

The announcement was made by the EU's Ambassador to India, Jean-Eric Paquet.
India–EU FTA negotiations began in 2007, were suspended in 2013 and relaunched in 2022; the EU is India's largest trading partner in goods.

Examine its significance for India's trade diversification and strategic autonomy, and analyse the sticking points — particularly European carbon and sustainability measures — that could shape its implementation.

stories.headline: Suspected Ukrainian sea drones hit Russian warship at Libya's Benghazi base
stories.summary: Suspected Ukrainian sea drones struck the Russian navy corvette Merkury at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, severely damaging the vessel and igniting a fire at the facility, according to two Libyan military officials. Libya's eastern-based government said the ship had docked at Benghazi to take on fuel and supplies while returning to Russia. No party has publicly claimed responsibility, and the extent of damage and any casualties remain unconfirmed. If confirmed as a Ukrainian operation, the strike would mark an extension of the Russia-Ukraine war's maritime dimension into the southern Mediterranean and raise questions about Russia's naval logistics and military presence in Libya.
stories.whyItMatters: It illustrates two recurring UPSC themes at once — how cheap unmanned systems are reshaping naval warfare, and how the Russia-Ukraine conflict is spilling over into third countries and regions far from the original theatre.

static.topic: Sea drones (Unmanned Surface Vessels) and asymmetric naval warfare
static.syllabusNode: Security — Role of external state and non-state actors; Science and Technology — indigenisation and emerging defence technology
static.whatIsIt: Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs), or 'sea drones', are remotely piloted or autonomous boats that can carry sensors, weapons or explosive warheads for surveillance, mine countermeasures or one-way attack missions.
static.background: Naval drones moved from experimental to combat-proven after 2022, when Ukraine — lacking a large conventional navy — paired domestically produced USVs with anti-ship missiles to contest Russia's Black Sea Fleet, repeatedly striking ships and forcing the fleet to disperse from western Black Sea ports.
static.geography: First demonstrated at scale in the Black Sea; the reported Benghazi incident would extend the phenomenon to the southern Mediterranean.
static.whyInNews: Suspected Ukrainian sea drones reportedly damaged the Russian corvette Merkury at Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya.
static.wayForward: For India, the episode strengthens the case for accelerating indigenous USV programmes, developing harbour and anchorage defences against small surface and aerial drones, and evolving doctrine for swarm and asymmetric maritime attacks.
prelimsPointers: USVs are unmanned boats that may be remotely piloted or autonomous, used for surveillance, mine countermeasures or explosive strikes.
Ukraine has relied heavily on USVs and anti-ship missiles to challenge Russia's numerically superior Black Sea Fleet.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how unmanned systems are altering the character of naval warfare and what capability, doctrinal and legal responses they demand from a navy such as India's.

static.topic: Libya's protracted conflict and foreign intervention
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of the policies of developed and developing countries on India's interests; instability in India's extended neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: Since 2014 Libya has been split between a UN-recognised Government of National Unity based in Tripoli in the west and a rival eastern administration in Benghazi backed by the Libyan National Army.
static.background: The 2011 NATO-backed uprising that ended Muammar Gaddafi's rule was followed by civil war. A 2020 ceasefire and subsequent UN-facilitated political process failed to reunify state institutions, and rival external backers — including Turkey, Russia, Egypt and the UAE — have sustained the division.
static.geography: North Africa, on the southern Mediterranean coast; Benghazi is the principal city of eastern Libya (Cyrenaica), while Tripoli lies in the west.
static.socioEconomic: Control of oil fields and export terminals is central to the power struggle; prolonged conflict has degraded infrastructure and living standards and made Libya a major transit point for Mediterranean migration.
static.whyInNews: A Russian warship was reportedly struck while refuelling at Benghazi, spotlighting the foreign military presence in eastern Libya.
static.wayForward: An inclusive UN-facilitated political settlement, unification of rival security forces and an end to external arms transfers remain the only durable route out of the stalemate.
prelimsPointers: Libya's capital is Tripoli; Benghazi in the east is the seat of the rival eastern administration.
Libya holds the largest proven oil reserves in Africa and lies astride the central Mediterranean migration route.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how external intervention has shaped Libya's post-2011 trajectory and what it reveals about sovereignty and state-building in weak states.

static.topic: Spillover of the Russia-Ukraine war and Russia's African footprint
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India; effect of major-power policies on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: The Russia-Ukraine war has extended beyond Europe through sanctions, energy and food-market shocks, proxy competition, and Russian military and mercenary deployments across Africa and West Asia.
static.background: Russia has deepened security ties with several African states, notably through the Wagner Group — now restructured under Russian control — in Libya, Sudan, Mali and the Central African Republic, alongside arms supply and grain diplomacy.
static.geography: Mediterranean Sea and the Sahel–North Africa belt.
static.whyInNews: A suspected Ukrainian attack on a Russian warship in Libya suggests the war's naval dimension is reaching the Mediterranean.
static.wayForward: India, which has consistently urged dialogue and diplomacy, must balance its long-standing Russia ties, its expanding Western partnerships and its energy, trade and diaspora interests in the region.
prelimsPointers: The Mediterranean connects to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits — the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles — governed by the 1936 Montreux Convention.
Libya is a member of OPEC and of the African Union.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse how the Russia-Ukraine conflict is reshaping great-power competition in Africa and the Mediterranean, and assess India's options in that contested space.

prelims: Benghazi, in eastern Libya, hosts a naval base and is the seat of the country's eastern administration; Tripoli is the capital and seat of the UN-recognised Government of National Unity.
The Merkury is a Russian navy corvette — a small, fast, comparatively lightly armed warship class.
Sea drones are Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs); Ukraine has used them extensively against Russia's Black Sea Fleet.

stories.mainsQuestion: The reported drone attack on a Russian warship at Benghazi shows how unmanned systems and proxy competition are pushing the Russia-Ukraine conflict beyond Europe. Examine the implications for maritime security and for India's strategic interests in the Mediterranean and North Africa.

stories.headline: Bangladesh unrest: nearly 30 Awami League-linked houses burned after two BNP men killed
stories.summary: Bangladeshi reports describe arson targeting about 30 properties tied to Awami League figures as unrest widened, with The New Indian Express and India Today connecting the burnings to the killing of two BNP men and BNP–Awami League clashes. static.topic: India's Foreign Policy & Strategic Autonomy

static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks. It engages across the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA simultaneously.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and Quad (with US, Japan, Australia) gained salience after 2017.
static.geography: South Asia; India shares a land border with Bangladesh through West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
static.socioEconomic: Neighbourhood instability can affect border management, trade, connectivity and people-to-people ties; Bangladesh is a major South Asian partner.
static.whyInNews: Violence in Bangladesh and Indian political reactions have renewed focus on India's neighbourhood diplomacy.
static.wayForward: India should pursue calm, people-centric neighbourhood diplomacy, encourage stability and minority safety through official channels, and avoid letting domestic political rhetoric dictate bilateral ties.

static.topic: India Semiconductor Mission and chip self-reliance
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — developments and their applications; indigenisation of technology; industrial policy
static.whatIsIt: The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) is the dedicated agency under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) tasked with building India's semiconductor and display manufacturing ecosystem under the Semicon India Programme.
static.background: The Semicon India Programme was announced in December 2021 with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore, offering fiscal support for fabrication, assembly-testing-packaging (ATMP/OSAT), compound semiconductors and design. ISM was created as a division of MeitY to implement it, and a Design Linked Incentive scheme was added to support fabless start-ups. In 2024 the government approved its first set of projects, including a fabrication plant at Dholera in Gujarat, an ATMP unit at Morigaon in Assam and Micron's ATMP facility at Sanand.
static.geography: Global chip-making is highly concentrated: Taiwan dominates leading-edge foundry, South Korea leads in memory, the Netherlands supplies EUV lithography (ASML), Japan supplies materials and equipment, the US leads in design, EDA tools and core IP, while China is the largest end-market for finished chips.
static.socioEconomic: Semiconductors rank among India's largest import categories by value; domestic fabrication is linked to electronics manufacturing jobs, digital sovereignty and resilience against supply-chain shocks.
static.whyInNews: The Nvidia–China scrutiny illustrates precisely why control over chip supply chains matters — the same logic driving India's push for domestic fabrication and trusted-partner technology tie-ups.
static.wayForward: Sustain incentive stability across policy cycles, build the ancillary ecosystem (speciality gases, chemicals, substrates, metrology), expand semiconductor talent pipelines, and pursue technology partnerships with trusted suppliers while keeping trade policy WTO-consistent.
prelimsPointers: ISM functions under MeitY; the Semicon India Programme was launched in December 2021 with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore.
ATMP stands for Assembly, Testing, Marking and Packaging — the back-end of the chip value chain.
India's first approved projects include a fabrication plant at Dholera (Gujarat) and an ATMP unit at Morigaon (Assam).
static.mainsAngle: How far can incentive-led industrial policy make India a credible participant in global semiconductor value chains? Discuss with reference to the India Semiconductor Mission.

static.topic: US–China technology rivalry and semiconductor export controls
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — effect of policies and politics of developed countries on India's interests; GS-III Science & Technology
static.whatIsIt: Export controls are unilateral or plurilateral restrictions on the sale of sensitive goods, software and technology. The US administers them through the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Entity List maintained by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) in the Department of Commerce.
static.background: US restrictions on semiconductor technology transfers to China tightened progressively — from the Entity List actions against ZTE and Huawei beginning in 2018, to the October 2022 rules covering advanced computing chips and chipmaking equipment, subsequently extended to AI accelerators and, in coordination with allies, to advanced lithography equipment. The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 simultaneously subsidised domestic US manufacturing.
static.geography: Key chokepoints sit in a handful of jurisdictions: the Netherlands (ASML's EUV lithography monopoly), Japan (photoresists and equipment), Taiwan (TSMC's leading-edge foundry) and South Korea (memory).
static.socioEconomic: Controls raise compliance costs, fragment technical standards and accelerate import-substitution drives in China and elsewhere; they also create secondary-sanction risk for third-country firms.
static.whyInNews: Treasury Secretary Bessent's remarks indicate continuing US scrutiny of Nvidia's chip sales to China, keeping export-control enforcement in the spotlight.
static.wayForward: India should hedge — build domestic capability, diversify suppliers and design partners, and negotiate technology partnerships while mapping exposure to secondary-sanction risk.
prelimsPointers: The Entity List is maintained by the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) under the Department of Commerce.

static.topic: AI chip technology and economic espionage

static.whatIsIt: Economic espionage refers to state-sponsored or state-tolerated acquisition of trade secrets, proprietary designs and dual-use technology. Advanced AI chips and their design IP are increasingly treated as strategic assets warranting counter-intelligence protection.
static.background: Concerns over technology transfer through espionage, talent recruitment programmes and supply-chain infiltration have grown alongside the strategic value of AI compute. Reporting on the Nvidia episode suggests intelligence interest in AI chip technology predates the current controversy, echoing earlier patterns of targeting semiconductor and defence know-how.
static.geography: Espionage risk concentrates at design hubs (US, Taiwan, South Korea), fabrication clusters and research universities, and along logistics routes for restricted hardware.
static.socioEconomic: Loss of IP erodes the returns on R&D investment, weakens export-control regimes and raises costs for legitimate firms through tighter compliance and screening.
static.whyInNews: Reports that Chinese intelligence targeted AI chips years before the Nvidia scandal surfaced add a national-security dimension to the export-control debate.
static.wayForward: Strengthen counter-intelligence screening in research and industry, tighten export-compliance auditing in firms, and build multilateral mechanisms for tracking diversion of dual-use technology.
prelimsPointers: AI accelerators such as GPUs are classified as dual-use items because of their military and intelligence applications.
Nvidia is a fabless US chip designer — it designs GPUs and AI accelerators but outsources fabrication to foundries such as TSMC.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the weaponisation of technology supply chains and economic espionage together challenge the global rules-based trading order.

stories.headline: Voters challenge SIR deletions in Karnataka, allege pressure to withdraw appeals
stories.summary: In Karnataka, voters whose names were deleted during the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) have challenged the deletions, alleging that officials asked them to withdraw appeals and instead file Form 6 for fresh enrolment; some said officials submitted Form 6 applications on their behalf. The reports highlight procedural confusion and pressure around the appeals process. Two opinion pieces in The Hindu argue that the SIR exercise reflects deeper problems with the ECI's use of centralised software, recalling the 2015 NERPAP Aadhaar-linkage effort halted by the Supreme Court, and contend that outdated manuals allow software to function as the rulebook. Together, the coverage raises questions about transparency, due process, and the right to vote in technology-driven electoral roll revision.
stories.whyItMatters: UPSC GS-II: electoral reforms, ECI powers, and governance; also links to data governance and digital public infrastructure debates.

static.topic: Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Elections, Electoral Reforms, Constitutional Bodies
static.whatIsIt: SIR is a special intensive revision of electoral rolls by the Election Commission of India, involving house-to-house or booth-level verification, deletion of dead, shifted, duplicate or ineligible electors, and enrolment of eligible persons.
static.background: Electoral rolls are prepared and revised under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. The ECI conducts annual and special revisions; SIR is an intensive, special drive to verify and update rolls, including deletion of ineligible entries and fresh enrolment.
static.geography: Karnataka (Bengaluru); SIR can be statewide or constituency-specific.
static.socioEconomic: Deletions can affect voting rights, welfare-linked documentation, and trust in electoral institutions; marginalised voters may face higher burdens in proving eligibility and pursuing appeals.
static.whyInNews: Voters in Karnataka challenged SIR deletions; reports allege officials asked them to withdraw appeals and file Form 6, with some Form 6 applications allegedly submitted by officials.
static.wayForward: Ensure reasoned deletion orders, accessible and independent appeals, prohibition of coercive re-enrolment, public dashboards of deletion and re-inclusion data, and periodic audit of software and manuals.

The ECI is a constitutional body under Article 324 of the Constitution.

static.mainsAngle: Examine how intensive electoral roll revisions can balance electoral integrity with the right to vote and procedural fairness, especially when technology mediates deletions and appeals.

static.topic: Digital Public Infrastructure and Data Governance in Electoral Rolls

static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure includes Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs processing of personal data. Electoral roll management increasingly uses software for deduplication, verification and roll revision.
static.background: Aadhaar (UIDAI, 2009) is the world's largest biometric ID; UPI (NPCI, 2016) processes billions of monthly transactions; the DPDP Act, 2023 introduces consent-based processing and a Data Protection Board. static.geography: India
static.socioEconomic: Digital exclusion and error propagation can disenfranchise voters; privacy risks arise when biometric or identity data is linked to electoral rolls.
static.whyInNews: Opinion pieces argue the ECI's software use needs reconsideration and that the SIR exercise is also a technology failure.
static.wayForward: Adopt auditable algorithms, human-in-the-loop appeals, updated manuals, data-protection safeguards, and independent audits before large-scale deletions.
prelimsPointers: The DPDP Act, 2023 provides for consent, data-principal rights, and significant data fiduciaries.
Aadhaar is operated by UIDAI; UPI is operated by NPCI.
The opinion piece recalls that the 2015 NERPAP Aadhaar-voter ID linkage was halted by the Supreme Court.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the benefits and risks of using digital public infrastructure and data-driven tools in electoral roll management, with reference to privacy, due process and disenfranchisement.

Form 6 is for new voter enrolment; Form 7 for deletion or objection; Form 8 for correction or shifting.

stories.headline: Russian strike kills two near Kyiv; Baltic vessel towed after drone hit
stories.summary: A Russian attack overnight struck a five-storey apartment building in Dymer, a settlement in Kyiv Oblast north of the Ukrainian capital, with rescue teams evacuating nine people including a child from the rubble. Wire reports differed on the toll, with some outlets reporting two dead and four wounded and others reporting three killed, while around eleven people were feared trapped; such divergence is typical of early casualty reporting from conflict zones. Separately, Finland said Russia had begun towing a vessel that was hit by drones in the Baltic Sea, an incident that extends the maritime dimension of the war into NATO-adjacent waters. The Kaliningrad region also sounded a rare air alert, underscoring how the conflict's spillover is being felt along Russia's western periphery. Together the strikes and the Baltic episode point to a war that is simultaneously intensifying on Ukrainian territory and widening geographically.
stories.whyItMatters: The episode illustrates two recurring UPSC themes: the paralysis of the UN Security Council in the face of a P5 member's own conduct, and the spillover of European land war into Baltic and NATO-adjacent maritime space.

perspectives.take: Frames the Dymer strike through the humanitarian lens — rescuers pulling nine survivors, including a child, from a destroyed residential block with eleven feared trapped; also flags the rare air alert in Kaliningrad as a sign of widening spillover.

static.topic: UN Security Council Reform and the Veto in the Russia-Ukraine War
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance / United Nations & Multilateral Reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the continuing strikes on Ukrainian cities have repeatedly exposed the veto's capacity to block Council action against a P5 member itself.
static.geography: UN Headquarters in New York; the International Court of Justice sits at The Hague.
static.socioEconomic: Council paralysis on Europe's largest land war since 1945 weakens the credibility of collective security guarantees on which smaller states rely, and pushes middle powers towards plurilateral and minilateral arrangements.
static.whyInNews: Continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian urban centres, including the Dymer apartment block, revive the question of why the Security Council cannot act against a permanent member.
static.wayForward: Revive text-based negotiations in the Intergovernmental Negotiations, build cross-regional coalitions beyond the G4 (including the African Group and L.69), and pursue interim steps such as a voluntary veto restraint on mass-atrocity situations.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN HQ is in New York.
The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) jointly campaigns for permanent UNSC seats.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim rests on representativeness, its population and contributions; assess obstacles such as veto politics and the Africa's Ezulwini Consensus.

static.topic: Russia-Ukraine War and Baltic Sea Security
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of Policies and Politics of Developed and Developing Countries on India's Interests
static.whatIsIt: The full-scale Russia-Ukraine war that began in February 2022 has evolved into a protracted attritional conflict with a growing maritime and drone-warfare dimension, now extending into the Baltic Sea and Russia's Kaliningrad exclave.
static.background: After the 2014 annexation of Crimea and the conflict in eastern Ukraine, Russia's February 2022 invasion triggered sweeping Western sanctions, large-scale military assistance to Kyiv, and the expansion of NATO to Finland and Sweden. The Baltic Sea became a NATO-dominated water body, making incidents there strategically sensitive.

static.socioEconomic: The war has disrupted global energy, foodgrain and fertiliser markets, affected shipping and insurance costs, and shaped India's own energy-import and diplomatic balancing choices.
static.whyInNews: A Russian strike on an apartment building near Kyiv killed civilians, while Finland reported that Russia had begun towing a drone-damaged vessel in the Baltic and Kaliningrad sounded a rare air alert.
static.wayForward: For India, the imperative is to sustain strategic autonomy, press for diplomacy and de-escalation, protect energy and food security interests, and continue humanitarian and reconstruction-linked engagement without being drawn into bloc politics.

stories.headline: Tamil Nadu moves Supreme Court review against Karthigai Deepam interim order
stories.summary: Tamil Nadu has filed a review petition in the Supreme Court against an interim order that allowed the lighting of lamps at the Deepathoon during the Karthigai Deepam observance at Thiruparankundram, near Madurai. The state's core objection is procedural: it argues that the interim arrangement, by permitting the lighting before the underlying dispute is finally adjudicated, in effect grants final relief at an interlocutory stage. In a related plea, petitioners before the court sought an interim stay on the lighting at the Deepathoon. The matter therefore turns on how the apex court calibrates interim relief that may be irreversible in practice, and on whether the review bench reconsiders the interim directions. The dispute remains sub judice.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the doctrine that interim orders should preserve the status quo rather than deliver the final relief, and illustrates the Supreme Court's review jurisdiction under Article 137 in politically and socially sensitive temple-related disputes.

perspectives.take: Leads with the state's legal argument that the Supreme Court granted final relief at the interim stage, framing the review petition as a corrective against premature adjudication.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: structure of the higher judiciary, judicial review, writ and review powers
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power of courts to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction; Article 137 separately empowers the Supreme Court to review its own judgments and orders.
static.whyInNews: Tamil Nadu has invoked the Supreme Court's review jurisdiction against an interim order permitting lamp lighting at the Deepathoon during Karthigai Deepam at Thiruparankundram, arguing that final relief was effectively granted at the interim stage.
static.wayForward: Clarify through judicial practice the standards for granting interim relief in disputes of a religious or irreversible nature, and address pendency and vacancy pressures that encourage early, decisive interlocutory orders.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court lies in disputes between the Centre and states (Article 131); advisory jurisdiction is under Article 143.
Article 137 lets the Supreme Court review any judgment pronounced or order made by it, subject to any law made by Parliament.
static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial backlog, vacancies and pendency; and the balance between judicial independence and accountability in the higher judiciary.

static.topic: Review Jurisdiction and Interim Relief in Constitutional Litigation
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: review petitions, interlocutory orders and the doctrine against final relief at an interim stage
static.whatIsIt: A review petition asks the same court to reconsider its own judgment or order, and is distinct from an appeal. Interim orders are interlocutory directions meant to preserve the status quo or balance convenience until the case is finally heard.
static.background: Article 137 confers the review power on the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court Rules, 2013 (Order XLVII) codify review procedure: a review petition is ordinarily heard by circulation in chambers, without oral argument, unless the court directs otherwise, and is generally placed before the same combination that passed the order. Where review fails, a curative petition remains the last resort in limited circumstances.
static.whyInNews: The review petition turns on the contention that an interim direction allowing lamp lighting amounted to the final relief, prompting the plea that such an order be reconsidered and, separately, that lighting at the Deepathoon be stayed.
static.wayForward: Courts could articulate clearer tests for interim relief where the relief is practically irreversible — such as heightened scrutiny, reasoned findings on prima facie case, irreparable harm and balance of convenience — so that interlocutory orders do not pre-empt final adjudication.
prelimsPointers: Review lies to the same court that passed the order and is not an appeal on merits.
Review petitions are normally decided by circulation in chambers, without oral hearing, unless the court permits oral arguments.
static.mainsAngle: Interim orders that effectively grant final relief can short-circuit adjudication in sensitive disputes. Discuss the standards courts should apply, with reference to the Supreme Court's review jurisdiction.

prelims: Tamil Nadu has filed a review petition in the Supreme Court against an interim order permitting lamp lighting at the Deepathoon during Karthigai Deepam at Thiruparankundram, near Madurai.

Review under Article 137 is a power of the Supreme Court to reconsider its own judgment or order; it is distinct from an appeal.

stories.mainsQuestion: Interim orders that in effect grant the final relief can defeat the very purpose of adjudication in socially sensitive disputes. Examine this proposition in the light of the Supreme Court's review jurisdiction under Article 137, and suggest standards that courts should apply before granting such interim relief.

stories.headline: FSSAI moves to prosecute Bisleri over unsafe packaged drinking water
stories.summary: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has ordered prosecution against Bisleri International after a sample of its packaged drinking water was found non-compliant with prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The regulator's action, reported first by wire services and detailed by The Hindu, marks a rare instance of the apex food authority escalating a quality failure against a leading packaged water brand to criminal prosecution rather than routine penalty. The finding centres on bromate, a disinfection by-product formed when ozone is used to treat water containing bromide, and one that is classified as possibly carcinogenic to humans. The case puts the spotlight on enforcement capacity, testing infrastructure and the certification chain that governs India's fast-growing packaged drinking water market.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live case study on the working of a statutory regulator (FSSAI) and on how food-safety standards, BIS certification and prosecution provisions under the FSS Act actually operate in practice. Useful for GS-II governance/statutory bodies and GS-III health, environment and consumer-protection questions.

perspectives.take: Frames the development as a corporate-legal event — India's food regulator taking a major bottled-water company to court — with a wire-service emphasis on the action and its business implications rather than the technical standard breached.

Domestic, detail-oriented framing: foregrounds the regulator's own statement that the sample breached prescribed bromate limits and was declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006, anchoring the story in Indian food-safety law.

static.topic: FSSAI and the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Statutory and Regulatory Bodies; Government Policies and Interventions
static.whatIsIt: FSSAI is India's apex food regulator, a statutory body constituted under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, functioning under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. It lays down science-based standards for food articles, regulates their manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import, and works through State Food Safety Commissioners and designated officers for licensing, sampling and enforcement.
static.background: The FSS Act, 2006 consolidated a fragmented set of earlier laws — including the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, the Fruit Products Order, 1955, the Meat Food Products Order, 1973, the Vegetable Oil Products Order, 1947, the Edible Oils Packaging Order, 1988 and the Milk and Milk Products Order, 1992 — into a single regulatory framework. FSSAI was established under the Act and became operational in 2008. The Act provides for sampling and analysis by notified laboratories, adjudication by Adjudicating Officers, and prosecution for offences such as manufacturing or selling unsafe food.
static.socioEconomic: Food-safety enforcement affects public health outcomes, consumer trust and the viability of a large organised food-processing and packaged-beverage industry, much of it MSME-based.
static.whyInNews: FSSAI has ordered prosecution against Bisleri International after a packaged drinking water sample was found non-compliant with prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006.
static.wayForward: Strengthen testing laboratory density and accreditation, publish sampling and prosecution data transparently, and shift from episodic enforcement to risk-based, third-party-audited surveillance of high-risk food categories.
prelimsPointers: FSSAI is a statutory body under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; it became operational in 2008.
The FSS Act, 2006 consolidated several earlier food laws, including the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
The Act distinguishes between 'substandard' and 'unsafe' food, with graded penalties and provision for prosecution.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's food-safety regime suffers from a standards deficit or an enforcement and capacity deficit, using recent regulatory action against packaged food and beverage brands as evidence.

static.topic: Packaged Drinking Water: BIS Certification and Bromate Standards
static.syllabusNode: Environment and Ecology — Water Quality and Pollution; Science and Technology — Health and Standards
static.whatIsIt: Packaged drinking water in India is regulated jointly: FSSAI prescribes food-safety standards under the FSS Act, while the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) certifies the product under IS 14543 (packaged drinking water other than mineral water) and IS 13428 (packaged natural mineral water). Manufacturers require a valid BIS licence in addition to FSSAI compliance.
static.background: Bromate is a disinfection by-product formed when ozone is used to disinfect water containing naturally occurring bromide. It is classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), and the WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality set a guideline value of 10 micrograms per litre. FSSAI has, in recent years, tightened oversight of the packaged water sector, including classifying packaged drinking water and mineral water as high-risk food categories requiring mandatory audits and BIS certification.
static.geography: Relevant across urban and peri-urban India, where demand for packaged water is driven by gaps in the reliability and quality of municipal piped supply.
static.socioEconomic: Packaged drinking water is a large and rapidly expanding consumer market with numerous small and regional players; compliance costs and testing access weigh disproportionately on smaller units, while consumers face information asymmetry about quality.
static.whyInNews: A Bisleri sample was found to exceed prescribed bromate limits, prompting FSSAI to declare it unsafe and order prosecution.
static.wayForward: Mandatory periodic testing for disinfection by-products, tighter control of ozonation processes at bottling plants, public disclosure of test results, and stronger surveillance of unbranded and small-scale packaged water units.
prelimsPointers: Bromate forms when ozone is used to disinfect water containing bromide; WHO's guideline value for bromate in drinking water is 10 micrograms per litre.
IARC classifies bromate as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B).
Packaged drinking water is certified by BIS under IS 14543; packaged natural mineral water under IS 13428.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the public-health and regulatory challenges posed by disinfection by-products in packaged drinking water and suggest a risk-based compliance framework for the sector.

static.topic: Food Safety as a Rights-Based Public Health Guarantee
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare, Rights and Public Health
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare architecture blends rights-based legislation with delivery mechanisms. The FSS Act, 2006 is the safety counterpart to the National Food Security Act, 2013, which addresses food availability and access; together they frame food as a matter of both entitlement and safety, with the right to health read into Article 21.
static.background: Rights-based laws such as MGNREGA (2005), the RTE Act (2009) and the NFSA (2013) shifted welfare from discretion to entitlement, supported by DBT and the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) backbone. Consumer protection law, including the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the CCPA, provides a parallel remedy channel for defective and unsafe goods.
static.socioEconomic: Unsafe food and water impose a disproportionate health and productivity burden on low-income households, who also have the least ability to verify quality or seek redress.
static.whyInNews: The FSSAI prosecution order against a major packaged water brand illustrates how food-safety enforcement translates a statutory guarantee into consumer protection.
static.wayForward: Link food-safety enforcement with consumer redress mechanisms, expand public testing and information access, and integrate food-safety surveillance into primary health reporting.
prelimsPointers: The National Food Security Act, 2013 addresses food access and entitlement, while the FSS Act, 2006 addresses food safety.
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 established the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA).
static.mainsAngle: Examine how effectively India's rights-based welfare framework extends to food safety and consumer protection for vulnerable groups.

prelims: FSSAI is a statutory body under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; it became operational in 2008.

The FSS Act, 2006 distinguishes 'substandard' from 'unsafe' food and provides for prosecution of manufacturers, sellers and distributors of unsafe food.

Examine whether the gap lies in the legal standards or in the enforcement architecture, and suggest reforms for risk-based regulation of high-risk food categories.

stories.headline: Tata Steel to sell two downstream units to APL Apollo for ₹28,000 crore
stories.summary: Tata Steel has announced a ₹28,000-crore agreement to sell two of its downstream steel businesses to APL Apollo Tubes, in what would rank among the largest private-sector asset transfers in Indian steel in recent years. The transaction is positioned by the company as a value-unlocking move, allowing it to concentrate capital on its core integrated steelmaking and upstream operations while paring exposure to lower-margin, more competitive downstream segments. For APL Apollo, already a leading player in structural steel tubes, the acquisition would sharply expand capacity and product range, consolidating its position in the value-added steel products market. Market coverage of the announcement framed it as part of a broader week of corporate action, including regulatory tightening on algorithmic trading and fresh order wins across infrastructure and renewables counters. The deal will require the usual clearances, including competition scrutiny, before it is consummated.
stories.whyItMatters: Large-ticket consolidation in steel is a live case study for UPSC on industrial policy, competition regulation and corporate restructuring, and it feeds directly into questions on the National Steel Policy's capacity targets and India's asset-monetisation push.

perspectives.take: Frames the sale as a value-unlocking exercise by Tata Steel, placing it within a market wrap that also flags regulatory tightening on algo trading and a mixed week for Indian equities.

static.topic: Indian Steel Industry and the National Steel Policy, 2017
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Infrastructure: Energy, Ports, Roads, Airports, Railways; Industry and Industrial Policy
static.whatIsIt: India is among the world's largest crude steel producers, with an integrated upstream segment (iron ore to crude steel) and a fragmented downstream segment producing tubes, pipes, cold-rolled and galvanised products. The National Steel Policy, 2017 sets the long-term direction for capacity, technology and raw-material security.
static.background: The modern Indian steel industry traces to the Tata Iron and Steel Company, set up in 1907 at Jamshedpur, followed by public-sector plants at Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur and Bokaro in the post-Independence era. Liberalisation in 1991 opened the sector to private and foreign participation, and the sector is today largely deregulated with 100% FDI permitted through the automatic route. The National Steel Policy, 2017 was adopted to guide capacity expansion, and a Production Linked Incentive scheme for specialty steel was introduced in 2021 to reduce import dependence in high-grade categories.
static.geography: Steel capacity is concentrated in mineral-rich belts — Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka — while downstream tube and pipe units cluster closer to consumption markets in the National Capital Region, Gujarat and Maharashtra.
static.socioEconomic: The sector is a major employer and a heavy consumer of iron ore, coal and power; downstream value addition typically carries lower capital intensity but thinner margins and sharper competition than integrated steelmaking.
static.whyInNews: Tata Steel's ₹28,000-crore sale of two downstream units to APL Apollo Tubes illustrates the ongoing split between capital-heavy upstream steelmaking and competitive, value-added downstream product businesses.
static.wayForward: Policy attention remains on meeting the National Steel Policy capacity target, securing coking coal and scrap availability, expanding specialty steel output, and ensuring that consolidation does not reduce competition in downstream product markets.
prelimsPointers: The National Steel Policy, 2017 targets 300 million tonnes of crude steel capacity by 2030-31.
India permits 100% FDI in the steel sector through the automatic route.
Tata Iron and Steel Company was established in 1907 at Jamshedpur.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the separation of upstream steelmaking from downstream value-added businesses affects the competitiveness and capacity trajectory of India's steel sector.

static.topic: Asset Monetisation and Strategic Disinvestment
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Government Budgeting; Investment Models; Resource Mobilisation
static.whatIsIt: Asset monetisation involves transferring the rights to operate or own existing assets to private entities to unlock capital for fresh investment, while disinvestment refers to the sale of government equity in public-sector enterprises. Both are instruments of resource mobilisation and efficiency improvement.
static.background: The National Monetisation Pipeline was announced in August 2021 by NITI Aayog, covering core infrastructure assets across sectors over a multi-year period. The New Public Sector Enterprises Policy, 2021 classified sectors as strategic and non-strategic and envisaged minimal presence of the state in strategic sectors. Disinvestment is administered by the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management under the Ministry of Finance.
static.socioEconomic: Monetisation and disinvestment shift risk and operational responsibility to private balance sheets, potentially improving asset utilisation while raising concerns about pricing, job continuity and the creation of private monopolies.
static.whyInNews: The Tata Steel–APL Apollo transaction is a private-sector parallel to the value-unlocking logic that underpins India's asset monetisation and portfolio-pruning strategies.
static.wayForward: Transparent valuation, clear regulatory oversight and reinvestment of proceeds into capacity creation are the standard conditions for such transactions to deliver net economic gains.
prelimsPointers: The National Monetisation Pipeline was launched in August 2021 by NITI Aayog.
DIPAM functions under the Ministry of Finance and handles government disinvestment.
The New Public Sector Enterprises Policy, 2021 was announced as part of the Atmanirbhar Bharat package.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether asset monetisation and portfolio pruning by both public and private enterprises can improve capital allocation without harming competition or employment.

static.topic: Competition Commission of India and Merger Control
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Statutory, Regulatory and Quasi-Judicial Bodies
static.whatIsIt: The Competition Commission of India is the statutory authority that enforces the Competition Act, 2002, prohibiting anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominance, and reviewing combinations that cross prescribed asset or turnover thresholds.
static.background: The Competition Act, 2002 replaced the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act framework, and the Commission became functional in 2009. The Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduced a deal-value threshold for notifying combinations and shortened the review timeline, strengthening the merger-control regime.
static.socioEconomic: Merger control balances the efficiency gains of consolidation against the risk of concentrated market power, which matters especially in intermediate goods markets such as steel tubes and pipes.
static.whyInNews: A transaction of this scale in the downstream steel segment would typically require scrutiny under India's combination regulations before completion.
static.wayForward: Continued capacity building of the regulator, timely approvals and clear guidance on deal-value thresholds will determine how smoothly large industrial consolidations proceed.
prelimsPointers: The Competition Commission of India became functional in 2009 under the Competition Act, 2002.
The Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduced a deal-value threshold for notifying combinations.
The Commission is a quasi-judicial body; appeals lie to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether India's merger-control framework is adequately equipped to handle rapid consolidation in core industrial sectors.

prelims: Tata Steel has agreed to sell two downstream units to APL Apollo Tubes in a deal valued at ₹28,000 crore.
APL Apollo Tubes is a major Indian producer of structural steel tubes, a downstream value-added steel product.
The National Steel Policy, 2017 targets 300 million tonnes of crude steel capacity by 2030-31.
Large combinations in India are reviewed by the Competition Commission of India under the Competition Act, 2002.
stories.mainsQuestion: Large-scale asset sales by integrated steel producers are being presented as value-unlocking exercises. Examine the implications of such consolidation for competition, employment and the achievement of India's steel capacity targets.

stories.headline: Sitharaman column claims a decade of poverty reduction, pitches barrier-removal over relief
stories.summary: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, writing in a column reproduced and amplified across outlets, argued that the past decade marks a structural break in India's poverty story — a shift from short-term relief handouts to dismantling the barriers that reproduce poverty. The piece credits welfare delivery reform, direct benefit transfers and the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) backbone with improving the reach and durability of anti-poverty support. It is a government framing of the record rather than an independent evaluation, and it leans on multidimensional poverty estimates rather than a fresh consumption-based poverty line. The claim therefore invites scrutiny of measurement choices, of quality of employment, and of whether gains are durable across states and social groups.
stories.whyItMatters: Poverty measurement and welfare design sit at the intersection of GS-II social justice and GS-III inclusive growth, and the government's own framing shapes future expenditure and scheme design.

perspectives.take: Carries the Finance Minister's op-ed in her own voice, framing the decade as a deliberate doctrinal shift from relief to removing structural barriers to upward mobility — a government-side argument, not an independent assessment.
Reports the same column as a news item, foregrounding the official claim of a decade 'turning the tide' with limited interrogation of the underlying poverty-line methodology.

static.topic: Poverty, Inequality & Employment
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Inclusive Growth, Poverty and Employment
static.whatIsIt: India tracks poverty through NITI Aayog's National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and through household consumption surveys, while employment is tracked by the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS).
static.background: NITI Aayog's National MPI, first released in 2021, uses 12 indicators across health, education and standard of living, aligned to the global Alkire-Foster method. Consumption-based poverty lines date to the Tendulkar and Rangarajan committees; no official poverty line has been published since the 2011-12 consumption survey. PLFS has run since 2017, reporting quarterly urban and annual all-India data.
static.geography: Inter-state disparities persist; the 2021 MPI baseline showed the highest multidimensional poverty in Bihar, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh, with the lowest in Kerala and Goa.
static.socioEconomic: A large share of the workforce remains informal and outside social security, so measured poverty reduction coexists with vulnerability to health and income shocks.
static.whyInNews: The Finance Minister's column claims a decade-long structural turn in poverty reduction, making measurement and welfare design a live policy debate.
static.wayForward: Publish a transparent, updated consumption-based poverty line; pair MPI gains with employment-quality indicators; extend social security portability to informal and urban migrant workers.
prelimsPointers: National MPI uses 3 dimensions and 12 indicators: health, education and standard of living.
Unemployment Rate = unemployed persons / labour force; LFPR = labour force / population.
PLFS has been conducted by NSO since 2017; urban data is released quarterly.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether India's poverty reduction is structural or consumption-driven, and examine the quality-of-employment and skills gap that limits inclusive growth.

static.topic: Welfare Architecture & Social Justice
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare Schemes, Rights and Delivery
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare model combines rights-based legislation with DBT-enabled schemes delivered through the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) trinity.
static.background: Rights-based laws include MGNREGA (2005), the Right to Education (2009) and the National Food Security Act (2013). Ayushman Bharat (2018) has an insurance arm (PM-JAY) and Health and Wellness Centres; POSHAN Abhiyaan targets malnutrition. Four labour codes consolidate 29 central labour laws.
static.socioEconomic: DBT reduces leakage and ghost beneficiaries but can create exclusion errors where Aadhaar seeding, bank access or digital literacy is weak — a recurring finding in welfare evaluations.
static.whyInNews: The column presents the shift from relief to barrier-removal as the core achievement of the decade, making welfare architecture the policy instrument under discussion.
static.wayForward: Strengthen grievance redress for exclusion errors, widen the tax-financed social security floor, and integrate health insurance with primary care rather than hospitalisation alone.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 central labour laws.
NFSA 2013 covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's welfare shift from entitlement to capability has reduced exclusion errors and urban poverty, and suggest institutional correctives.

prelims: NITI Aayog's National MPI (2021) measures deprivation across 3 dimensions and 12 indicators.
MGNREGA (2005) guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
PLFS, conducted by the National Statistical Office since 2017, is the primary source for LFPR and unemployment rates.
No official consumption-based poverty line has been published since the 2011-12 survey; MPI is the government's headline poverty metric.
stories.mainsQuestion: The government claims that the last decade shifted anti-poverty policy from relief to removing structural barriers. Critically examine this claim with reference to measurement methods, welfare delivery and the quality of employment in India.

stories.headline: Myanmar rejects ASEAN peace-plan review as Rohingya await justice after ICJ verdict
stories.summary: Myanmar's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected the review and recommendations on the ASEAN Five-Point Consensus adopted at the bloc's summit in Manila, calling them 'unfair and imbalanced' and complaining that they ignore the positive steps it claims to have taken, while also questioning how the grouping treats it. The pushback deepens the deadlock over ASEAN's 2021 peace plan, which has failed to halt violence or open humanitarian access since the February 2021 coup. In parallel, the ICJ's genocide verdict in the case concerning the Rohingya has revived hopes among displaced Rohingya families, including those in India, that host states will treat them with greater humanity. Many Rohingya in India remain undocumented, detained or labelled 'infiltrators', and face deportation despite having fled the 2017 military crackdown in Rakhine State. The two developments together frame the crisis as one of accountability versus regional diplomacy, with refugee protection caught in between.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the credibility of ASEAN's consensus-based diplomacy against a member state's defiance, and of international adjudication in delivering accountability for mass atrocities. Also directly relevant to India's refugee policy, non-refoulement obligations and its balancing act between Myanmar, ASEAN and human-rights scrutiny.

perspectives.take: Human-rights and refugee-centred framing: foregrounds an individual Rohingya survivor's story, criticising India's 'infiltrator' labelling, detention and deportation risk after the ICJ genocide verdict; advocacy-oriented, South Asia civil-society lens.

Diplomatic-reporting framing: reports Myanmar's official rejection of the ASEAN review as 'unfair and imbalanced' and its questioning of the bloc's treatment, giving the junta's stated position prominence alongside the regional deadlock.

static.topic: United Nations, ICJ and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and International Institutions
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. The International Court of Justice, the principal judicial organ, sits at The Hague and settles disputes between states and gives advisory opinions. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and among the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for Security Council expansion, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) remain inconclusive. The Genocide Convention of 1948 allows a state party to approach the ICJ over alleged genocide by another state party — the route used in the case against Myanmar, in which provisional measures were ordered in January 2020.
static.geography: The Hague, Netherlands (ICJ seat); ASEAN Secretariat in Jakarta; Rakhine State, Myanmar.
static.socioEconomic: Atrocity crimes in Rakhine triggered large-scale displacement into Bangladesh and onward movement across the region, creating protracted refugee and humanitarian burdens.
static.whyInNews: Myanmar rejected the ASEAN review of the Five-Point Consensus adopted at the Manila summit, and the ICJ's genocide verdict has renewed debate on accountability and refugee protection.
static.wayForward: Strengthen atrocity-prevention mechanisms, press for full implementation of ICJ orders, and pursue Security Council reform so that accountability does not depend on veto politics; India can leverage its standing with both ASEAN and Myanmar to keep humanitarian access on the table.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent (veto) + 10 elected for two-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus on Myanmar was agreed in April 2021.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether consensus-based regional organisations like ASEAN can deliver on peace and accountability when a member state defies them, and assess the limits of international adjudication without enforcement powers.

static.topic: India's Refugee Policy and Non-Refoulement
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Welfare Schemes, Laws and Institutions; International Relations — Diaspora and Refugees
static.whatIsIt: India has no dedicated domestic refugee law. Persons fleeing persecution are dealt with under the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 and the Citizenship Act, 1955, while UNHCR operates in India under its own mandate to register and assist certain refugee groups.
static.background: India is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol, though it has historically hosted large refugee populations — Tibetans from 1959, Sri Lankan Tamils from the 1980s, and Chakmas. Rohingya arrivals increased sharply after the 2017 military crackdown in Rakhine State; many have been detained, and some deported, with courts intervening in individual cases.
static.geography: Rakhine State (Myanmar), Cox's Bazar (Bangladesh), and Rohingya settlements in India including Jammu, Hyderabad and Delhi-NCR.
static.socioEconomic: Detention, lack of documentation and denial of work and education push displaced families into informality and vulnerability, while host communities raise concerns over resources and security.
static.whyInNews: After the ICJ genocide verdict, Rohingya refugees in India — including the family of a man who fled persecution — hope for more humane treatment instead of being branded 'infiltrators' and detained.
static.wayForward: Enact a domestic refugee framework with clear status-determination procedures, uphold the principle of non-refoulement in line with India's human-rights commitments, and ensure access to basic services and legal aid for the displaced.
prelimsPointers: India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol.
UNHCR carries out refugee status determination in India under its mandate, not under Indian law.
The principle of non-refoulement bars returning a person to a territory where they face serious harm.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether India's absence of a domestic refugee law is compatible with its constitutional and international human-rights obligations, using the Rohingya experience as a case study.

prelims: ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus on Myanmar was agreed in April 2021 and includes ending violence, constructive dialogue and humanitarian access.
The ICJ, the principal judicial organ of the UN, sits at The Hague and hears disputes between states; the Genocide Convention, 1948, is the basis of the case against Myanmar.
India is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol, and has no dedicated domestic refugee law.
ASEAN has 10 member states and takes decisions by consensus, which limits its ability to enforce compliance on a member.
stories.mainsQuestion: Consensus-based regional diplomacy and international adjudication have both struggled to resolve the Myanmar crisis. Critically examine the limits of ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus and the ICJ route in delivering accountability and protection for the Rohingya, and outline what India's response should be.

stories.headline: Israel coalition talks stall as settler arson draws condemnation
stories.summary: Coalition negotiations between Likud, led by Benjamin Netanyahu, and the party of Gadi Eisenkot ended without an agreement, leaving Israel's next government unresolved. Likud reportedly laid down conditions for a unity arrangement that included keeping Arab parties out of the coalition and rejecting a Palestinian state, while Eisenkot, who holds the mandate to form a government, faces a 6 December deadline. Separately, Eisenkot condemned arson attacks by Jewish settlers in the West Bank, calling them 'Jewish terrorism' that endangers lives, undermines regional stability and damages Israel's national security and foreign relations. Together, the two developments signal both a deepening domestic political deadlock and the diplomatic costs of settler violence, with the talks expected to resume.
stories.whyItMatters: Israel's coalition arithmetic and the West Bank settler question are the two domestic variables that most constrain any revival of the West Asia peace process — directly relevant to GS-II International Relations and to India's Israel–Palestine balancing act.
