static.topic: Israel's coalition politics and government formation
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Comparative Politics & West Asia
static.whatIsIt: Israel elects its legislature, the Knesset, by proportional representation, so no single party has ever commanded a majority on its own; governments are always coalitions and a working majority requires 61 of 120 seats. The President, after consulting parties, assigns the mandate to form a government to a member who is expected to muster that majority, and the mandate is time-bound.
static.background: Israel has no single written constitution; it is governed through a set of Basic Laws that define the Knesset, the government and the presidency. Because proportional representation produces many small parties, coalition-building — and the conditions partners extract — has repeatedly determined the country's policy direction, including on the Palestinian question.
static.geography: Israel lies on the eastern Mediterranean, bordered by Lebanon and Syria in the north, Jordan in the east and Egypt in the south-west, with the West Bank and Gaza as Palestinian territories.
static.socioEconomic: Coalition bargains typically trade religious, settlement and budgetary concessions for seats, giving small parties disproportionate leverage over national policy.
static.whyInNews: Likud and Eisenkot's party ended a round of unity talks without a deal, with Likud's reported conditions — no Arab parties and no Palestinian state — narrowing the room for compromise before the 6 December mandate deadline.
static.wayForward: Watch whether the mandate holder can assemble 61 seats, whether the talks resume on softened terms, or whether a further election becomes the only exit from the deadlock.
prelimsPointers: The Knesset has 120 members; a governing coalition needs 61 seats.
Israel has no single written constitution and is governed by Basic Laws.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how proportional representation and coalition compulsions shape Israel's foreign-policy flexibility, especially on the Palestinian question.

static.topic: Israeli settlements in the West Bank and international law
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — West Asia & International Law
static.whatIsIt: Settlements are Israeli civilian communities established in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, territories occupied by Israel since 1967. Most states and UN bodies regard them as illegal under the Fourth Geneva Convention, which bars an occupying power from transferring its own population into occupied territory.
static.background: Israel captured the West Bank and East Jerusalem in the 1967 Six-Day War. UN Security Council Resolution 242 (1967) established the 'land for peace' framework; the Oslo Accords (1993) created the Palestinian Authority and divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C; UNSC Resolution 2334 (2016) reaffirmed that settlements have no legal validity and constitute a flagrant violation of international law.
static.geography: The West Bank lies west of the Jordan River, with East Jerusalem and the Jordan Valley as its most contested zones; Area C, under full Israeli civil and security control, holds most settlement infrastructure.
static.socioEconomic: Settlement expansion fragments Palestinian land, restricts movement and access to water and farmland, and raises the recurring cost of violence and military protection for Israel.
static.whyInNews: Eisenkot described arson attacks by Jewish settlers in the West Bank as 'Jewish terrorism', warning that such groups are undermining regional stability, endangering lives and damaging Israel's national security and foreign relations.
static.wayForward: Any durable settlement freeze or rollback would require both coalition politics in Jerusalem to permit it and a credible political horizon for the Palestinians, without which the two-state framework erodes further.
prelimsPointers: UNSC Resolution 2334 (2016) stated that Israeli settlements have no legal validity.
The Oslo Accords (1993) provided for mutual recognition between Israel and the PLO and created the Palestinian Authority.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how settler violence and settlement expansion affect the viability of the two-state solution and the wider West Asia peace process.

static.topic: UN Security Council and multilateral responses in West Asia
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive. In West Asia, repeated use of the veto in the Council has stymied binding action and pushed debate towards the General Assembly and regional diplomacy.
static.whyInNews: Deadlock in Israel's government formation and continuing settler violence in the West Bank keep the Palestinian question on the international agenda, reviving questions about the Security Council's effectiveness and the veto.
static.wayForward: For India, the reform case rests on representativeness and contributions; meanwhile it must balance its Israel and Palestine ties through humanitarian assistance and principled support for a two-state solution.
prelimsPointers: The UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for two-year terms.
The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent UNSC membership rests on representativeness, its population and contributions; assess the obstacles — veto politics and the African Ezulwini Consensus.

stories.mainsQuestion: Domestic political fragmentation and settler violence in the occupied territories both constrain Israel's strategic choices. Examine the implications for the West Asia peace process and for India's interests in the region.

stories.headline: NGT notice to Environment Ministry over 'forever chemicals' contamination
stories.summary: The National Green Tribunal has issued a notice to the Union Environment Ministry in a matter concerning contamination by per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), the synthetic compounds widely called 'forever chemicals'. The tribunal's intervention follows concern that these substances — used in non-stick cookware, firefighting foams, textiles and food packaging — persist in the environment and accumulate in living organisms, even as India lacks a comprehensive domestic standard governing them. The notice seeks the ministry's response and signals judicial scrutiny of the regulatory gap on emerging contaminants. TheWire.in reported the development, framing it as a test of institutional accountability on chemical pollution.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the NGT's role as India's specialised environmental tribunal and exposes the regulatory vacuum on emerging contaminants — a recurring GS-III theme linking pollution control, chemical safety and international conventions.

perspectives.take: Frames the notice as regulatory accountability — a tribunal pulling the Environment Ministry up over an unregulated contamination risk; environment-focused, civil-liberties-leaning outlet that foregrounds state inaction.

static.topic: National Green Tribunal (NGT)
static.syllabusNode: Statutory, Regulatory and Quasi-Judicial Bodies
static.whatIsIt: A specialised statutory tribunal created under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, for the effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to environmental protection, conservation of forests and other natural resources, enforcement of legal rights relating to the environment, and relief and compensation for damage to persons and property.
static.background: Established by the NGT Act, 2010, India is among the few countries with a dedicated environmental tribunal. It has a Principal Bench at New Delhi and zonal benches at Pune (Western), Bhopal (Central), Kolkata (Eastern) and Chennai (Southern). It comprises a Chairperson and judicial and expert members, and is guided by the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
static.geography: Principal Bench at New Delhi; zonal benches at Pune, Bhopal, Kolkata and Chennai.
static.socioEconomic: Environmental disputes frequently pit livelihood-dependent communities against industry, making compensation, restitution and access to speedy justice central to the tribunal's socio-economic role.
static.whyInNews: The NGT has issued a notice to the Union Environment Ministry over contamination by 'forever chemicals' (PFAS).
static.wayForward: Strengthen the tribunal's technical capacity and enforcement of its orders, and pair judicial intervention with statutory standards for emerging contaminants so that regulation does not depend on litigation alone.
prelimsPointers: The NGT was set up under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, and is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but is guided by principles of natural justice.
Appeals against NGT orders lie to the Supreme Court; the tribunal's jurisdiction covers environmental protection, forests and natural resources.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the NGT's effectiveness in enforcing environmental regulation, and examine whether judicial intervention can substitute for a robust statutory framework on emerging contaminants.

static.topic: PFAS and 'Forever Chemicals'
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Environmental Pollution and Degradation
static.whatIsIt: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a large family of synthetic organofluorine chemicals built on exceptionally strong carbon–fluorine bonds, which make them highly resistant to degradation — hence the term 'forever chemicals'. They are used in non-stick coatings, firefighting foams, stain- and water-repellent textiles, and food packaging, and are associated with persistence, bioaccumulation and long-range transport.
static.background: Concern over PFAS has been channelled through the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, to which India is a Party. Specific PFAS — including PFOS, PFOA and PFHxS — have been brought under the Convention's listing and phase-out or restriction regimes. In India, chemical pollution is regulated principally through the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and rules framed under it, along with the Water Act, 1974 and the Air Act, 1981, but there is no comprehensive PFAS-specific standard.
static.socioEconomic: Contamination is typically concentrated around fluorochemical manufacturing sites, firefighting training grounds and industrial clusters, exposing workers and nearby communities through drinking water and food chains.
static.whyInNews: The NGT has issued a notice to the Environment Ministry over PFAS contamination, highlighting the absence of a domestic regulatory framework for these substances.
static.wayForward: Build monitoring and testing capacity, set drinking-water and discharge limits for PFAS under existing environmental law, phase out the most hazardous compounds in line with international listings, and adopt a precautionary approach pending full toxicological data.
prelimsPointers: PFAS are called 'forever chemicals' because the strong carbon–fluorine bond makes them extremely resistant to natural breakdown.
The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants is the principal international instrument listing and restricting PFAS such as PFOS, PFOA and PFHxS.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss why emerging contaminants such as PFAS escape India's pollution-control framework, and suggest regulatory and institutional reforms to address them.

prelims: PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) are synthetic organofluorine compounds termed 'forever chemicals' because their carbon–fluorine bonds resist degradation.
The National Green Tribunal is a statutory body under the NGT Act, 2010, with a Principal Bench at New Delhi and zonal benches at Pune, Bhopal, Kolkata and Chennai.
The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants is the key international instrument under which certain PFAS have been listed for restriction or elimination.
India's principal legal handle on chemical pollution remains the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, supplemented by the Water Act, 1974 and the Air Act, 1981.
stories.mainsQuestion: The 'forever chemicals' problem illustrates the gap between India's environmental law framework and emerging contaminants. Examine this gap and evaluate the role of the National Green Tribunal in addressing it.

stories.headline: AMR Awareness Week: Europe's farm antibiotic focus wavers as prevention costs mount
stories.summary: World AMR Awareness Week (18–24 November) has renewed attention on antimicrobial resistance as a slow-moving but expensive public-health crisis. Down To Earth's coverage argues that money spent now on infection prevention, surveillance and antibiotic stewardship is far cheaper than the future bill for treating resistant infections. A second strand of the reporting asks whether Europe — long the global leader on curbing veterinary antibiotics after banning growth promoters in 2006 — is losing momentum on its farm-antibiotic reduction goals. Both pieces converge on the One Health point that human, animal and environmental antibiotic use form a single problem, with agricultural use now a major driver of resistance. The framing shifts AMR from a hospital prescribing issue to a food-system and development-finance issue.
stories.whyItMatters: AMR is a recurring UPSC theme linking GS-II health policy, GS-III science and technology, and agriculture and animal husbandry. The One Health framing, the economics of prevention versus treatment, and India's National Action Plan on AMR are frequently tested.

perspectives.take: Frames AMR as an economic choice — prevention and stewardship spending today versus far larger treatment and productivity costs later; a development and global-South lens.
Second piece questions whether Europe is drifting from its farm-antibiotic reduction agenda, treating the EU's 2006 growth-promoter ban and Farm to Fork targets as a benchmark now under strain.

articles.title: AMR Awareness Week: Pay now for prevention, or pay far more later for resistance
AMR Awareness Week: Is Europe losing its focus on reducing farm antibiotic use?

static.topic: Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) and the One Health approach
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Health and Biotechnology; Environment — One Health
static.whatIsIt: AMR occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites evolve to withstand medicines that once killed them, making common infections harder or impossible to treat. It is driven by overuse and misuse of antimicrobials in human medicine, animal husbandry and agriculture, poor infection control, and environmental spread of resistant organisms and residues.
static.background: The WHO Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2015, urging member states to prepare national action plans. India's National Action Plan on AMR (2017–2021) is coordinated by the National Centre for Disease Control, supported by a National AMR Surveillance Network. India's Red Line campaign (2016) marked prescription-only antibiotics to discourage over-the-counter use. World AMR Awareness Week, earlier called World Antibiotic Awareness Week, is observed from 18 to 24 November.
static.geography: Global in scope; India's surveillance covers a network of tertiary-care laboratories, with state-level initiatives such as Kerala's antibiotic literacy campaign often cited as models.
static.socioEconomic: Resistant infections raise treatment costs and length of hospital stay, pushing households towards catastrophic health expenditure. The World Bank has warned that unchecked AMR could cause substantial losses in global GDP and push millions into poverty by 2050, with low- and middle-income countries bearing the heaviest burden.
static.whyInNews: AMR Awareness Week coverage, including Down To Earth's argument that prevention spending now is cheaper than resistance later, and its question on whether Europe is losing focus on reducing farm antibiotic use.
static.wayForward: Strengthen AMR surveillance and laboratory capacity, enforce prescription-only dispensing, regulate antibiotic use in poultry and aquaculture, curb pharmaceutical manufacturing effluent, expand vaccination and diagnostics, and institutionalise One Health coordination across health, agriculture and environment ministries.
prelimsPointers: World AMR Awareness Week is observed annually from 18 to 24 November.
The WHO Global Action Plan on AMR was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2015.
India's National Action Plan on AMR (2017–2021) is coordinated by the NCDC.
The EU banned antibiotic growth promoters in farm animals in 2006.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why AMR is called a silent pandemic and assess the adequacy of India's surveillance, regulatory and stewardship architecture in a One Health framework.

static.topic: Antibiotic use in livestock and agri-food systems
static.paper: GS-III (Agriculture and Animal Husbandry); also GS-II Health
static.syllabusNode: Agriculture — Animal Husbandry and Food Safety; Health — Zoonoses and Food-borne Resistance
static.whatIsIt: Routine administration of antibiotics to farmed animals — for growth promotion, disease prevention (prophylaxis) and group treatment of sick animals (metaphylaxis) — creates reservoirs of resistant bacteria that can reach humans through food, water, soil, farm workers and the wider environment.
static.background: The European Union banned antibiotic growth promoters in farm animals in 2006 and later adopted Regulation 2019/6 on veterinary medicinal products, applicable from 2022, which prohibits routine prophylactic use and restricts metaphylaxis. The EU's Farm to Fork strategy targets a 50 per cent reduction in sales of antimicrobials for farmed animals and aquaculture by 2030, with the European Medicines Agency's ESVAC reports tracking sales. In India, antibiotic use is widespread in poultry and aquaculture, and FSSAI has notified maximum residue limits for antibiotics in meat and meat products.
static.geography: Europe has historically led on veterinary antibiotic reduction; India's rapidly growing poultry, dairy and aquaculture sectors are the emerging front line.
static.socioEconomic: Smallholder livestock and poultry producers depend on cheap antibiotics for productivity and income, so restrictions must be paired with affordable alternatives; residue and resistance concerns also affect export competitiveness of meat, milk and seafood.
static.whyInNews: Down To Earth's AMR Awareness Week piece asks whether Europe is losing its focus on reducing farm antibiotic use, making agricultural stewardship the centre of the debate.
static.wayForward: Phase out growth-promotion use, make veterinary antibiotics prescription-only, monitor sales and residues, promote vaccines, probiotics, improved biosecurity and hygiene, and support farmers with transition costs.
prelimsPointers: The EU banned antibiotic growth promoters in farm animals in 2006.
The EU Farm to Fork strategy targets a 50 per cent cut in sales of antimicrobials for farmed animals and aquaculture by 2030.
The European Medicines Agency publishes ESVAC reports on veterinary antimicrobial sales.
FSSAI has notified maximum residue limits for antibiotics in meat and meat products.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how veterinary and agricultural antibiotic use fuels AMR, and suggest regulatory and market-based measures suited to India's livestock economy.

static.topic: Health financing and India's welfare architecture
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare & Rights
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare model blends rights-based laws (MGNREGA 2005, RTE 2009, NFSA 2013) with DBT-enabled schemes and a JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) delivery backbone.
static.background: Ayushman Bharat (2018) has a health-insurance arm (PM-JAY) and Health & Wellness Centres. POSHAN Abhiyaan targets malnutrition. Article 15/16 and Indra Sawhney (1992) frame reservation policy.
static.socioEconomic: AMR's economic burden — longer hospital stays, costlier second-line drugs and lost productivity — falls hardest on households with weak financial buffers. The 'pay now for prevention or pay more later' argument therefore connects directly to health financing, out-of-pocket expenditure and the reach of welfare delivery.
static.whyInNews: AMR Awareness Week's emphasis on prevention spending versus future resistance costs links antimicrobial policy to India's health-financing and welfare debate.
static.wayForward: Raise public health spending, strengthen primary care and infection prevention, and integrate AMR stewardship into existing welfare and insurance delivery channels to reduce catastrophic health expenditure.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 labour laws.
static.mainsAngle: Welfare exclusion errors, urban poverty, and the shift from entitlement to capability.

prelims: World AMR Awareness Week is observed annually from 18 to 24 November.
The EU banned antibiotic growth promoters in farm animals in 2006, and its Farm to Fork strategy targets a 50 per cent reduction in sales of antimicrobials for farmed animals and aquaculture by 2030.
The WHO Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2015; India's National Action Plan on AMR (2017–2021) is coordinated by the NCDC.
Antibiotic growth promoters are sub-therapeutic antibiotics given routinely to livestock to accelerate growth — a practice linked to the emergence of resistant bacteria.
stories.mainsQuestion: Antimicrobial resistance is often described as a 'silent pandemic'. Examine the contribution of agricultural and veterinary antibiotic use to AMR and evaluate whether India's regulatory, surveillance and One Health frameworks are adequate to address it.

stories.headline: Core sector output stays weak as oil and gas lag
stories.summary: India's eight core industries — coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement and electricity — continued to post subdued output, with the upstream oil and gas segments the weakest link. Even a favourable low base from the corresponding period a year earlier was not enough to lift crude oil and natural gas production into positive territory, suggesting structural supply constraints rather than a purely cyclical dip. Since these industries carry a combined weight of about 40% in the Index of Industrial Production, their weakness transmits directly into headline industrial and GDP growth readings. The editorial argues that the persistent drag in hydrocarbons deserves closer policy attention given India's heavy dependence on imported crude.
stories.whyItMatters: Core sector data is a leading indicator for IIP and GDP, and the oil-and-gas lag ties directly to energy security and the import bill — recurring GS-III themes in both prelims facts and mains analysis.

perspectives.take: Frames the slump as an accountability question: a low base should have flattered the numbers, so the oil and gas contraction points to deeper structural weakness; editorial tone is critical of policy follow-through.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.snippet: Even a low base effect could not push India’s oil and gas sectors into growth

static.topic: Eight Core Industries and the Index of Core Industries (ICI)
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Growth, Development and Industrial Policy; Infrastructure
static.whatIsIt: The Index of Eight Core Industries measures the combined and individual production performance of eight infrastructure-linked industries — coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement and electricity — and is published monthly.
static.background: These eight industries were designated 'core' because of their strong backward and forward linkages with the rest of the economy. The index is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and serves as a lead indicator for the Index of Industrial Production.
static.geography: Refining capacity is concentrated on the west coast (Gujarat, Maharashtra) with additional capacity on the east coast; crude oil and natural gas output is dominated by offshore western fields and the Assam–Arakan basin.
static.socioEconomic: These sectors underpin construction, transport, power and agricultural inputs; weakness here raises input costs, affects employment in capital-intensive industry and widens the hydrocarbon import bill.
static.whyInNews: The latest core sector print showed continued weakness, with crude oil and natural gas failing to grow even against a low year-ago base.
static.wayForward: Diversify crude sourcing, accelerate domestic exploration and production through licensing rounds, expand refining and petrochemical integration, and improve data granularity for timely policy response.
prelimsPointers: The eight core industries carry a combined weight of 40.27% in the IIP.
ICI is released by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
Refinery products have the highest individual weight within the index, followed by electricity and steel.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why core sector weakness persists despite policy support, and assess its implications for industrial growth and energy security.

static.topic: Base effect and the reading of high-frequency economic data
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Economic Growth, National Income and Data Interpretation
static.whatIsIt: The base effect is the distortion in a growth rate caused by the size of the reference period's value: a low base inflates measured growth, while a high base depresses it.
static.background: Base effects became a widely discussed issue in India after the pandemic-year contraction produced unusually high growth rates in the following year across IIP, GDP and core sector series.
static.socioEconomic: Misreading base-driven swings can lead to premature policy tightening or unwarranted optimism; analysts therefore track seasonally adjusted and sequential month-on-month data alongside year-on-year growth.
static.whyInNews: The editorial highlights that even a low base failed to push oil and gas output into growth, indicating the weakness is structural rather than statistical.
static.wayForward: Use seasonally adjusted series, multi-year CAGR and sequential comparisons for a more robust read of underlying momentum.
prelimsPointers: A low base makes year-on-year growth look higher; a high base suppresses it.
IIP and core sector data are monthly high-frequency indicators, typically released with roughly a month's lag.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how base effects distort the interpretation of India's high-frequency data and what statistical practices can mitigate the problem.

prelims: The Index of Eight Core Industries covers coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement and electricity, with a combined weight of 40.27% in the IIP.
It is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
A low base effect inflates year-on-year growth, while a high base suppresses it.
Refinery products carry the largest weight among the eight core industries, followed by electricity and steel.
stories.mainsQuestion: Core sector weakness has persisted despite a favourable base. Examine the structural constraints in India's oil and gas sector and suggest measures to strengthen the core industrial base.

stories.headline: Green India Mission: timely funds and robust monitoring key to climate goals
stories.summary: An editorial in The Hindu examines the National Mission for a Green India (Green India Mission), one of the eight missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change, and argues that it has functioned more as a paper commitment than a delivery mechanism. The core criticism is that climate action of this kind requires funds to be released on time, in adequate volume, and backed by credible monitoring of outcomes rather than only of expenditure. The piece situates the mission's weak performance within the wider gap between India's stated climate and restoration ambitions and the institutional capacity to execute them. It implies that without ring-fenced financing, clear outcome indicators and periodic public reporting, afforestation and forest-quality targets will remain unmet.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-III environment questions on NAPCC missions, climate finance and forest governance, and to GS-II questions on the monitoring and accountability of flagship government schemes.

perspectives.take: Frames the Green India Mission as a 'paper tiger' — a mission whose climate objectives are undermined by delayed and inadequate funding and by weak monitoring, and calls for time-bound, resource-backed implementation.

articles.title: Paper tiger: On the Green India Mission
articles.snippet: Climate action has to be timely, with adequate resources and monitoring

static.topic: Green India Mission and India's climate commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change; Conservation and Climate Governance
static.whatIsIt: The National Mission for a Green India (Green India Mission) is one of the eight national missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008). It seeks to increase forest and tree cover, improve the quality of existing forest cover, and enhance forest-based livelihoods for forest-dependent communities. The editorial questions whether its funding and monitoring architecture is equal to these objectives.
static.background: The NAPCC was launched in 2008, with the Green India Mission as its forestry and ecosystem mission. The mission was approved by the Union Cabinet in 2014 with a multi-year outlay for the Twelfth Plan period. Its mission document sets out targets of increasing forest/tree cover on 5 million hectares and improving the quality of forest cover on another 5 million hectares, alongside livelihood benefits for about 3 million households. Implementation has been repeatedly flagged for slow fund utilisation and weak outcome measurement.
static.geography: Operates across diverse forest landscapes — Himalayan region, Western Ghats, central Indian forests, mangroves and coastal ecosystems — where restoration potential and community dependence are both high.
static.socioEconomic: Forest-dependent communities, joint forest management institutions and FRA-recognised gram sabhas are central to implementation; afforestation outcomes are tied to livelihood income, fuelwood, fodder and non-timber forest produce.
static.whyInNews: A The Hindu editorial ('Paper tiger') argues that the Green India Mission needs timely and adequate resources and credible monitoring if climate action is to move beyond announcements.
static.wayForward: Ring-fence and front-load mission funds, converge with compensatory afforestation and CAMPA resources, adopt landscape-level planning, publish outcome-based indicators (survival rates, canopy improvement, carbon and livelihood gains) and institutionalise third-party and community monitoring.
prelimsPointers: The NAPCC (2008) comprises eight national missions, including the National Solar Mission, National Water Mission, National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem and the Green India Mission.
India's updated NDC targets a 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels by 2030 and 50% of installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate why India's climate missions underperform at the implementation stage, and examine the role of financing certainty, institutional capacity and outcome monitoring in translating climate pledges into measurable results.

static.topic: Forest and biodiversity conservation framework in India
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Biodiversity and Conservation
static.whatIsIt: India's conservation architecture rests on the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, the Biological Diversity Act 2002 and the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), now guided by the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) and its 30x30 target. The Green India Mission's restoration goals sit within this framework.
static.background: The Ramsar Convention (1971) governs wetland protection and India has more than 80 Ramsar sites. Project Tiger (1973) and Project Elephant (1992) anchor species conservation. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) commits parties to protecting 30% of land and sea by 2030.
static.geography: India is one of 17 megadiverse countries; its recognised biodiversity hotspots are the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).
static.socioEconomic: Conservation must be balanced against community rights under the Forest Rights Act and against rising human-wildlife conflict, making restoration a socio-economic as well as ecological exercise.
static.whyInNews: The editorial's concern about weak delivery of afforestation and forest-quality targets bears directly on India's ability to meet its biodiversity and restoration commitments.
static.wayForward: Landscape-level restoration planning, control of invasive species, community-led regeneration through gram sabhas and JFMCs, and transparent reporting against 30x30 and national restoration pledges.
prelimsPointers: India's biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).
World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February; India has more than 80 Ramsar sites.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how afforestation and restoration missions can be aligned with biodiversity goals and community rights, and assess the adequacy of India's monitoring of conservation outcomes.

static.topic: Parliamentary oversight and accountability of flagship missions
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament and Legislative Process; Governance and Accountability
static.whatIsIt: Parliament authorises and scrutinises public expenditure, and Departmentally Related Standing Committees examine the working of ministries and their schemes. This oversight machinery is the institutional route through which concerns about under-funded or weakly monitored missions can be examined.
static.background: Parliament under Article 79 comprises the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; a Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111). Money Bills (Article 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha. Ordinances (Article 123) must be approved within six weeks of Parliament reassembling. Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise Bills and ministry performance.
static.whyInNews: The editorial's demand for better monitoring of the Green India Mission points to the wider question of how Parliament and its committees hold mission-based climate spending to account.
static.wayForward: Strengthen committee scrutiny of mission-wise expenditure and outcomes, mandate outcome-based reporting in demand-for-grants discussions, and improve the quality of data placed before Parliament.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Assess the effectiveness of parliamentary committees in scrutinising scheme implementation and expenditure, and suggest reforms to strengthen legislative oversight of climate and environmental missions.

prelims: The Green India Mission is one of the eight missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008), which also includes the National Solar Mission, National Water Mission and the National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem.
India's updated NDC: 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels by 2030; 50% of installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030; net zero by 2070.
Forest and tree cover accounts for roughly a quarter of India's geographical area, as reported in the India State of Forest Report.
Compensatory afforestation in India is governed by the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016, with CAMPA funds used for afforestation and restoration activities.
stories.mainsQuestion: The Green India Mission is central to India's climate adaptation and restoration strategy, yet it has been criticised as under-funded and weakly monitored. Examine the reasons for its implementation gaps and suggest reforms in financing, monitoring and community participation to make afforestation missions deliver measurable outcomes.

stories.headline: Centre weighs sharing fertiliser subsidy burden with States
stories.summary: The Centre is reported to be examining a model under which the fertiliser subsidy burden would be shared with States, as the Union's subsidy outgo continues to rise. The proposal is being discussed in the context of pressure on central finances from a subsidy that is currently borne almost entirely by the Union government. States have historically resisted cost-sharing in centrally administered input subsidies, since fertiliser pricing and distribution are controlled by the Centre. If taken forward, the idea would mark a shift in how a key farm-input subsidy is financed and would raise fresh questions about fiscal federalism and the sustainability of input subsidies.
stories.whyItMatters: Fertiliser subsidy is one of the largest central revenue expenditures and a recurring GS-III theme on subsidy reform, fiscal deficit and agricultural input efficiency; any Centre–State cost-sharing proposal also directly tests GS-II federalism and fiscal devolution debates.

perspectives.take: Frames the move primarily as a fiscal-management exercise — the Centre exploring burden-sharing with States to contain a rising subsidy bill; a market-and-fiscal-prudence lens typical of business press.

articles.title: Centre considers fertiliser subsidy sharing model amid rising costs
articles.snippet: Centre considers fertiliser subsidy sharing model amid rising costs Business Standard

static.topic: Fertiliser subsidy and the Nutrient-Based Subsidy (NBS) regime
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Agriculture: input subsidies, farm economics and food security
static.whatIsIt: Fertiliser subsidy is a central budgetary support that keeps farm-gate prices of fertilisers below their cost of production/import. Urea remains under statutory price control with a fixed maximum retail price, while P&K fertilisers are covered by the Nutrient-Based Subsidy, under which a per-nutrient subsidy is notified and manufacturers fix MRPs. The subsidy is administered by the Department of Fertilizers and delivered largely through manufacturers/importers, with direct benefit transfer pilots for retail sales.
static.background: Fertiliser subsidy dates back to the Green Revolution era, when it was used to promote fertiliser use and foodgrain output. The Nutrient-Based Subsidy was introduced in 2010 for P&K fertilisers, shifting from product-based to nutrient-based support. Neem coating of urea was made mandatory in 2015 to curb diversion to non-agricultural uses. Direct Benefit Transfer for fertiliser sales was rolled out in phases from 2018 to plug leakages. Subsidy arrears to companies and the skewed urea-to-P&K consumption ratio have been recurring policy concerns.
static.socioEconomic: Fertiliser subsidy lowers the cost of cultivation for farmers but distorts the nutrient mix, encourages excessive urea use, and strains soil and water health. It is a large recurring drain on the Union budget and a source of working-capital stress for fertiliser firms when arrears build up.
static.whyInNews: The Centre is reported to be considering a model to share the fertiliser subsidy burden with States amid rising costs.
static.wayForward: Move towards nutrient-neutral, DBT-based subsidy delivery; rationalise urea price control in a phased manner; promote balanced fertilisation through Soil Health Cards; and settle any Centre–State cost-sharing through a clear, predictable framework rather than ad hoc burden transfer.
prelimsPointers: Urea remains under statutory price control with a fixed MRP; P&K fertilisers are governed by the Nutrient-Based Subsidy introduced in 2010.
Neem coating of urea was made mandatory in 2015 to prevent diversion for industrial use.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether shifting part of the fertiliser subsidy to States improves fiscal discipline or merely displaces the burden, and suggest reforms that align subsidy design with soil health and nutrient balance.

static.topic: Fiscal federalism and Centre–State resource sharing
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution: Centre–State fiscal relations
static.whatIsIt: India's quasi-federal scheme divides powers through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists in the Seventh Schedule, with residuary powers with the Union. Financially, the Union raises the bulk of revenues and shares them with States through Finance Commission recommendations, centrally sponsored schemes and Article 282 grants, making fiscal federalism a continuing negotiation.
static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre–State balance, including fiscal relations. The Finance Commission, constituted under Article 280, recommends vertical and horizontal devolution of the divisible pool. The GST Council (Article 279A) is a constitutional body for indirect tax coordination. Disputes over cesses and surcharges outside the divisible pool, and over the design of centrally sponsored schemes, have repeatedly strained cooperative federalism.
static.socioEconomic: States with weaker own-revenue bases depend heavily on central transfers; any new cost-sharing obligation without matching untied funds can squeeze State spending on health, education and rural infrastructure.
static.whyInNews: A reported proposal to share the fertiliser subsidy burden with States raises the question of whether the Union can unilaterally shift a centrally administered subsidy onto States.
static.wayForward: Any burden-sharing must be backed by predictable, untied transfers and prior consultation through intergovernmental forums; subsidy reform is better anchored in the Finance Commission cycle than in ad hoc cost transfers.
prelimsPointers: The Finance Commission is constituted under Article 280; the GST Council under Article 279A.
On a Concurrent List subject, a Union law prevails in case of repugnancy unless the State law has been reserved for and given the President's assent (Article 254).
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how unilateral shifts of centrally administered subsidy burdens affect cooperative federalism, and suggest institutional safeguards for Centre–State fiscal negotiation.

prelims: Fertiliser subsidy is a central sector expenditure; urea is under statutory price control with a fixed MRP, while P&K fertilisers are covered by the Nutrient-Based Subsidy introduced in 2010.
Neem coating of urea was made mandatory in 2015 to check diversion to non-agricultural uses.
Direct Benefit Transfer for fertiliser sales was rolled out in phases from 2018 to reduce leakages.
The Finance Commission (Article 280) recommends devolution of the divisible pool; the GST Council (Article 279A) is a constitutional body for indirect tax coordination.
stories.mainsQuestion: The proposal to share the fertiliser subsidy burden between the Union and States raises both fiscal and federal questions. Examine the implications for cooperative federalism and suggest a reform pathway that improves nutrient balance without weakening farmer welfare.

stories.headline: Akal Takht Jathedar seeks reopening of Kartarpur corridor; 1,822 Sikh pilgrims in Pakistan
stories.summary: The Akal Takht Jathedar, Gargaj, used a visit to Lahore to call for peace between India and Pakistan and for the reopening of the Kartarpur Corridor, the visa-free route that lets Indian Sikh pilgrims reach Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Pakistan's Narowal district. His appeal coincided with the departure of 1,822 Sikh pilgrims from India to Pakistan for Guru Nanak Dev's birth anniversary, a pilgrimage that has continued even though the corridor itself remains shut. In a parallel development, Pakistan's minister Masood Malik declined to answer questions on Pakistan's posture on the Indus waters and on the Pahalgam terror attack. The juxtaposition captures the two-track nature of the relationship: devotional travel and shrine diplomacy proceed, while the core security and water disputes stay frozen.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests understanding of India–Pakistan relations beyond the security binary — the Kartarpur Corridor as faith diplomacy, the Indus Waters Treaty as a live pressure point, and the limits of people-to-people contact when the political track is stalled.

perspectives.take: Reports the Jathedar's Lahore visit as a peace overture and, in a separate report, presses Pakistan's minister on the Indus waters threat and the Pahalgam attack — Indian mainstream, security-sceptical framing.
Leads with the pilgrim numbers and the ritual calendar, treating the movement as a religious-travel event rather than a diplomatic one — Delhi-centric and descriptive.

static.topic: Kartarpur Corridor and faith diplomacy between India and Pakistan
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; cultural and people-to-people diplomacy
static.whatIsIt: A visa-free cross-border passage of roughly 4.5 km linking Dera Baba Nanak in Gurdaspur district, Punjab (India) to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib at Kartarpur in Narowal district, Punjab (Pakistan) — the site where Guru Nanak Dev spent his final years.
static.background: The corridor was agreed through a Memorandum of Understanding in 2018 and inaugurated in November 2019 to mark the 550th birth anniversary of Guru Nanak Dev, despite the absence of a wider bilateral dialogue. Services were suspended from 2020 and have not been fully restored, though pilgrims have continued to travel for major gurpurabs through other arrangements.
static.geography: Dera Baba Nanak (Gurdaspur, Indian Punjab) to Kartarpur (Narowal, Pakistani Punjab); the corridor crosses the Ravi river and the international boundary.
static.socioEconomic: Punjab on both sides shares language, kinship and an agrarian economy; shrine tourism supports local livelihoods and is one of the few contact channels left when trade and travel are shut.
static.whyInNews: The Akal Takht Jathedar, on reaching Lahore, publicly sought the corridor's reopening, while 1,822 Sikh pilgrims travelled to Pakistan for Guru Nanak Dev's birth anniversary.
static.wayForward: Decouple the corridor from the political dispute through a standing operational protocol, restore pre-2020 frequency, and widen access to Nankana Sahib and other Sikh heritage sites.
prelimsPointers: The corridor connects Dera Baba Nanak (Gurdaspur, Punjab) with Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur (Narowal, Pakistan).
It was inaugurated in November 2019 on the 550th birth anniversary of Guru Nanak Dev.
The Akal Takht, in Amritsar, is the highest temporal seat of the Sikh faith.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether faith-based and people-to-people channels such as the Kartarpur Corridor can be insulated from the wider India–Pakistan security dispute.

static.topic: Indus Waters Treaty and water as leverage in India–Pakistan relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; bilateral treaties and water diplomacy
static.whatIsIt: A 1960 treaty between India and Pakistan, brokered by the World Bank, that allocates the Indus system: the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) are for India's use and the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) largely for Pakistan, with limited Indian use permitted.
static.background: Signed in Karachi in 1960 by Jawaharlal Nehru and Ayub Khan with World Bank mediation, it survived the 1965, 1971 and 1999 wars. It created the Permanent Indus Commission and a graded dispute-settlement mechanism — the Neutral Expert and, at a later stage, a Court of Arbitration. India has used the treaty's run-of-the-river provisions for projects such as Baglihar and Kishenganga. Following the Pahalgam terror attack of 2025, India held the treaty in abeyance.
static.geography: The Indus system rises in the Himalayas and Karakoram and flows through India (Ladakh, Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab) into Pakistan; the western rivers are the mainstay of Pakistan's agriculture.
static.socioEconomic: Pakistan's canal colonies and food security depend on the western rivers; Indian Punjab and Jammu and Kashmir depend on the eastern rivers and on limited western-river hydropower.
static.whyInNews: A Pakistani minister declined to answer questions on the Indus waters threat in the same week as the Kartarpur reopening appeal.
static.wayForward: Keep the Permanent Indus Commission's technical channel alive, avoid treating abeyance as a permanent posture, and pursue arbitration outcomes rather than escalation.
prelimsPointers: Eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas, Sutlej — are allocated to India; western rivers — Indus, Jhelum, Chenab — largely to Pakistan.
The treaty was brokered by the World Bank and signed in 1960.
Disputes go first to the Permanent Indus Commission, then a Neutral Expert, and then a Court of Arbitration.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the Indus Waters Treaty as an example of a durable bilateral water regime and assess the implications of holding it in abeyance.

static.topic: India–Pakistan relations: dialogue, cross-border terrorism and the stalled political track
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; bilateral relations
static.whatIsIt: The post-1947 bilateral relationship, structured by the Simla Agreement (1972), the Lahore Declaration (1999) and the Composite Dialogue, and repeatedly disrupted by cross-border terrorism.
static.background: Four wars (1947-48, 1965, 1971, 1999) and the 1971 creation of Bangladesh; the Simla Agreement committed both sides to bilateral resolution and treated the LoC as the de facto border. The 1999 Lahore Declaration and the 2004-2007 Composite Dialogue were followed by the 2008 Mumbai attacks and the 2016 Uri and 2019 Pulwama-Balakot episodes. Diplomatic ties were downgraded in 2019 and trade suspended; the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack led to Operation Sindoor and a further rupture.
static.geography: A long international boundary plus the Line of Control in Jammu and Kashmir; Punjab and Rajasthan share the longest stretches of the India–Pakistan border.
static.socioEconomic: Suspended trade, a closed Attari-Wagah crossing, divided families and the loss of pilgrim and cultural circuits.
static.whyInNews: The Akal Takht Jathedar's Lahore visit and the pilgrim movement sit alongside a Pakistani minister's refusal to engage on the Pahalgam attack.
static.wayForward: Separate the humanitarian and religious tracks from the security dispute, insist on verifiable action against terror infrastructure, and rebuild a narrow, issue-based dialogue.
prelimsPointers: The Simla Agreement (1972) committed India and Pakistan to resolving disputes bilaterally and made the LoC the de facto border in Jammu and Kashmir.
India withdrew Most Favoured Nation status to Pakistan in 2019.
The Attari-Wagah crossing in Punjab is the main land trade and passenger route between the two countries.
static.mainsAngle: Cross-border terrorism has repeatedly derailed India–Pakistan dialogue. Examine whether issue-based, people-centric engagement can coexist with a firm security posture.

prelims: 1,822 Sikh pilgrims left India for Pakistan to mark Guru Nanak Dev's birth anniversary.
The Akal Takht Jathedar, on reaching Lahore, called for peace and the reopening of the Kartarpur Corridor.
The Kartarpur Corridor links Dera Baba Nanak (Gurdaspur, India) to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur (Narowal, Pakistan).
Pakistan's minister Masood Malik did not respond to questions on the Indus waters threat and the Pahalgam attack.
stories.mainsQuestion: The Kartarpur Corridor and Sikh pilgrimage have remained a rare channel of contact between India and Pakistan even as the political and security tracks stay frozen. Examine the potential and the limits of faith-based diplomacy in India's Pakistan policy.

stories.headline: Tech outages push firms to reassess digital risk; US intelligence warns of more
stories.summary: A fresh wave of technology outages has disrupted business operations, prompting companies to treat continuity planning and third-party digital dependence as board-level risks rather than routine IT issues. Business Standard reports that firms are revisiting vendor concentration, failover systems and incident-response readiness, concluding that 'business as usual' is no longer viable. In parallel, the US intelligence chief has cautioned that further outages are likely as systems undergo upgrades, framing the problem as a structural feature of modernising digital infrastructure rather than a one-off failure. Taken together, the two accounts shift the debate from isolated glitches to systemic digital fragility across economies that now run on cloud, payment and identity platforms.
stories.whyItMatters: Cyber resilience of critical infrastructure and digital public platforms is a standing GS-III security theme and a GS-II e-governance concern; outage-driven disruption links directly to DPDP Act compliance and business-continuity obligations.

perspectives.take: Frames outages through a business-continuity and risk-management lens — firms must abandon 'business as usual' and rework operational resilience, vendor dependence and recovery planning.
Frames outages through a national-security and intelligence lens, reporting a US intelligence chief's prediction of more outages during system upgrades — a global, systemic-risk framing.

static.topic: Cyber Security and Critical Infrastructure Protection
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security: Cyber Security and Critical Infrastructure
static.whatIsIt: India's cyber-security architecture rests on CERT-In as the national nodal agency for incident response, NCIIPC for protecting critical information infrastructure, and the I4C initiative for coordinating cybercrime response, alongside NATGRID and Integrated Command and Control Centres supporting security operations.
static.background: CERT-In was set up in 2004 as the national computer emergency response team and issues advisories and incident-response directions; NCIIPC was created in 2015 under the NTRO to guard critical information infrastructure; the I4C (Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre) was established under the MHA to coordinate cybercrime response across states.
static.socioEconomic: Rising dependence on cloud services, payment rails and identity platforms means a single outage can cascade across banking, retail, health and government service delivery, imposing economic costs well beyond the affected firm.
static.whyInNews: Repeated technology outages have pushed firms to reassess digital risk, while a US intelligence chief predicted more such outages as systems undergo upgrades.
static.wayForward: Strengthen mandatory incident-reporting and uptime audits for critical operators, institutionalise third-party and supply-chain risk assessment, run periodic cross-sector outage drills, and build redundancy in payment and identity infrastructure.
prelimsPointers: CERT-In is the national nodal agency for cyber-incident response, functioning under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
NCIIPC, set up in 2015 under the NTRO, is the nodal agency for protecting critical information infrastructure.
I4C functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs to coordinate cybercrime response.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how India's cyber-security institutions must evolve from reactive incident response to anticipatory resilience, given the systemic risk posed by outages in critical digital infrastructure.

static.topic: Digital Public Infrastructure and Data Governance
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance and Data Governance
static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure — Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker — is a layered, interoperable stack, while the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs processing of personal data through consent-based mechanisms and a Data Protection Board.
static.background: Aadhaar, administered by UIDAI since 2009, is the world's largest biometric ID system; UPI, operated by NPCI since 2016, processes billions of monthly transactions; the DPDP Act, 2023 introduced consent-based processing, data-principal rights and obligations for significant data fiduciaries.
static.socioEconomic: Because DPI is interoperable and widely reused, availability failures at any layer can stall welfare transfers, payments and authentication for millions, making uptime a public-service obligation and not merely a commercial one.
static.whyInNews: Outage-driven disruption has turned attention to the resilience, availability and accountability of digital platforms on which both businesses and public service delivery depend.
static.wayForward: Build service-level and uptime obligations into DPI governance, mandate transparent outage disclosure and redress, align continuity planning with DPDP Act obligations on data fiduciaries, and preserve offline fallback channels for essential services.
prelimsPointers: NPCI operates UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH.
The DPDP Act, 2023 provides for consent, data-principal rights and obligations on significant data fiduciaries.
UIDAI administers Aadhaar; DigiLocker is a flagship paperless document-verification platform.
static.mainsAngle: Assess the tension between expanding DPI-based service delivery and the imperative of digital resilience, privacy and accountability under the DPDP Act framework.

prelims: CERT-In is India's national nodal agency for cyber-incident response, under MeitY.
NCIIPC (2015), under the NTRO, is the nodal agency for critical information infrastructure protection.
The DPDP Act, 2023 establishes a Data Protection Board and consent-based processing of personal data.
NPCI operates UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH, making payment-rail uptime a systemic concern.
stories.mainsQuestion: Technology outages are increasingly a governance and national-security challenge rather than a routine IT failure. Discuss the implications for India's digital public infrastructure and critical information infrastructure, and suggest institutional reforms for digital resilience.

stories.headline: ICE agents detain father, daughter at Seattle airport; governor calls agency 'out of control'
stories.summary: Masked federal immigration agents detained a father and his daughter on the jet bridge of an Alaska Airlines flight at a Seattle airport, delaying the departure while fellow passengers filmed the encounter on their phones. The family's lawyer said the two were travelling to attend a relative's baptism, and that the officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki trousers rather than identifiable uniforms. Washington State's governor publicly condemned the operation as evidence of an 'out-of-control' federal agency, and local television footage of the detention circulated widely. The episode has renewed debate in the United States over the visibility, accountability and state-level consent involved in federal immigration enforcement.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live case study in federal–state friction and accountability in enforcement agencies — themes that recur in comparative federalism, governance and migration questions in GS-II.

perspectives.take: Frames the episode through eyewitness shock — 'ICE is totally out of control' — emphasising masked agents dragging passengers off a jet bridge and the resulting flight delay.
Leads with the family's account: the lawyer says father and daughter were travelling to a relative's baptism, and notes officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants while passengers filmed.
Centres the political reaction, headlining the Washington governor's description of ICE as 'out-of-control' at Seattle airport — a state-versus-federal framing.
Local broadcast framing built on video evidence — 'appears to show' masked ICE agents detaining two passengers — prioritising verification of the footage.

static.topic: Federalism and the division of law-enforcement powers (India–US comparison)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided between the Union and States through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), with residuary powers vested in the Union under Article 248. The United States follows a different model in which states retain general police powers while immigration enforcement remains a federal function.
static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) examined the Centre-State balance in India. The Governor (Article 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and has been a recurring flashpoint over assent to Bills (Article 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Article 201).
static.geography: India, with a comparative reference to the United States
static.socioEconomic: Fiscal devolution and centrally sponsored schemes shape the practical bargaining power of States in India, just as funding and pre-emption shape state leverage in the US system.
static.whyInNews: Federal immigration agents detained two passengers at a Seattle airport over the objections of Washington State's governor, spotlighting how federal and sub-national authorities collide over enforcement powers.
static.wayForward: Strengthen institutionalised consultation mechanisms such as the Inter-State Council (Article 263) and codify timelines for the Governor's assent to reduce adversarial federalism.
prelimsPointers: On repugnancy in the Concurrent List, Union law prevails unless the State law has been reserved for and received the President's assent (Article 254).
The Inter-State Council (Article 263) is a recommendatory body for investigating and advising on inter-State disputes.
static.mainsAngle: Compare how India and the United States allocate and police the boundary between union and sub-national powers, and assess whether India's mechanisms for inter-governmental dispute resolution are adequate.

static.topic: US immigration enforcement architecture: ICE, DHS and sanctuary jurisdictions
static.syllabusNode: Governance & Accountability — institutional architecture (comparative)
static.whatIsIt: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is a federal agency within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) responsible for enforcing federal immigration and customs laws, including the detention and removal of non-citizens.
static.background: ICE was created in 2003 when the Homeland Security Act, 2002 reorganised federal agencies after the 9/11 attacks; immigration enforcement had earlier rested largely with the Immigration and Naturalization Service. The Immigration and Nationality Act, 1952 remains the principal governing statute. Some states and cities have declared themselves 'sanctuary' jurisdictions that limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
static.geography: United States
static.socioEconomic: Immigration enforcement intersects with labour markets, family unity and the rights of non-citizens; detention practices have repeatedly been litigated on due-process grounds.
static.whyInNews: The Seattle detention, filmed by passengers and criticised by Washington's governor, has renewed scrutiny of ICE's operational methods and its relationship with state and local authorities.
static.wayForward: Greater transparency in federal enforcement operations, clear identification of officers, and statutory clarity on state–federal cooperation are among the reform proposals debated in the United States.
prelimsPointers: ICE is a federal agency under the US Department of Homeland Security and was created in 2003.
Immigration enforcement is a federal function in the US; states retain general police powers under the Tenth Amendment.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how federal systems manage contested enforcement jurisdictions, with reference to immigration enforcement in the United States.

static.topic: India–US relations and the Indian diaspora
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World; Diaspora
static.whatIsIt: India and the United States maintain a Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership spanning defence, trade, technology, energy and people-to-people ties, with the Indian diaspora in the US among the largest and most influential Indian communities abroad.
static.background: The civil nuclear agreement (2005–2008), India's designation as a Major Defence Partner (2016) and cooperation through the Quad have deepened the relationship. Consular protection of Indian nationals abroad is a recurring diplomatic concern.
static.geography: India and the United States
static.socioEconomic: Remittances, skilled migration (H-1B visas) and student mobility are central to the economic dimension of the relationship.
static.whyInNews: The detention of travellers at US airports raises questions about the treatment of foreign nationals and the consular-protection responsibilities of Indian missions.
static.wayForward: Sustained consular outreach, diaspora grievance mechanisms and migration-mobility agreements can cushion the impact of stricter enforcement regimes.
prelimsPointers: India was designated a Major Defence Partner of the United States in 2016.
Consular access to detained foreign nationals is governed by the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, 1963.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how tightening immigration regimes in destination countries affect India's diaspora diplomacy and its consular obligations.

prelims: ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) is a federal agency of the US Department of Homeland Security, created in 2003.
Immigration enforcement in the United States is a federal responsibility; individual states cannot direct or veto federal operations.

stories.mainsQuestion: Federal enforcement agencies in the United States have increasingly operated within states that oppose their actions. Compare this with India's constitutional division of powers and evaluate the mechanisms each system provides for resolving union–state friction.
